articles.title_zh: A new 'Yalta'? Trump and Putin push for a meeting that Xi is wary of hosting

Donald Trump will meet Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China next week for an unprecedented three-way meeting between the leaders of the US , Russia , and China, with nuclear weapons and the war in Iran expected to be on the agenda.
The meeting will take place on Thursday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, the White House confirmed on Friday. It will bring together the leaders of the world’s three largest nuclear powers for the first time, although all three have held bilateral talks with one another.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The meeting comes nine months after the expiry of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), the last major nuclear arms control agreement between Washington and Moscow.
The treaty, which expired in February, had placed limits on the two countries’ strategic nuclear arsenals, leaving the world’s two largest nuclear powers without those restrictions for the first time in more than half a century.
Mr Trump has rejected Russia's offer to extend it for another year, saying he wanted a new agreement that would also include China.
Beijing has resisted joining such negotiations, arguing that its nuclear arsenal is much smaller than those of Washington and Moscow. China has more than 600 nuclear warheads, compared with more than 5,000 each for Russia and the US.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official told reporters, according to Reuters. “This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think ​it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have ​adult conversations about adult things.”
Mr Trump also intends to discuss the war in Iran with Mr Xi and Mr Putin, but Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is not expected to feature, the official said. “We’ve had many meetings ⁠recently with ​the Russians, but China is not really a part of that track, ​so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the official said.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly insisted that his country must be involved in any discussions about its future.
Russia had previously proposed the three-way meeting, with Mr Putin reportedly keen to use it to discuss Ukraine. The Russian president had floated the idea during a telephone conversation with Trump last month, according to the Wall Street Journal .
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha had warned against giving Putin such a platform. “Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandisement and give him a stature he does not deserve,” he said last month, adding that it would only “encourage Putin to continue this war”.
The planned summit has also drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the US, Britain, and the Soviet Union discussed the postwar settlement in Europe. The prospect of Mr Trump, Mr Putin, and Mr Xi meeting without Ukraine has revived concerns about major powers making decisions that affect other countries without consulting them.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the comparison, saying that any agreements reached in Shenzhen could not be imposed on other countries. He nevertheless described a meeting between the three leaders as “extremely significant”. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect,” he said.
Mr Trump is due to visit Manila on Tuesday for talks with leaders of the Association of South-east Asian Nations before heading to Shenzhen. He is also scheduled to hold bilateral talks and a working lunch with Xi on Thursday, ahead of the trilateral meeting.
The White House said billionaire Elon Musk would accompany Mr Trump on the China visit, but a senior US official said he would not attend the talks with Mr Xi and Mr Putin.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Netanyahu says it's time to remove Iran threat "once and for all"
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Netanyahu says it's time to remove Iran threat "once and for all"
articles.content_orig:
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi dismissed nine officials on Saturday, following an investigation into allegations of oil smuggling in the Jurf al-Sakher area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah group.
"In light of the investigation's findings," Zaidi "ordered that all individuals accused of involvement in oil smuggling operations be referred to the judiciary," his military spokesman Sabah al-Numan said, without identifying the suspects.
The premier "also ordered the dismissal" of nine officials including from the security and oil sectors.
The northern reaches of Iraq has several Shia Muslim militia groups that support Iran, a majority Shia country. The semi-autonomous groups have routinely launched missiles or drones at Middle Eastern countries in opposition to Iran's interests.
The U.S. and Saudi Arabia, a Sunni majority country and regular target of the Iraqi breakaway groups, launched joint strikes on northern Iraqi groups in July.
Invoking Iran's pursuit to rebuild its nuclear program, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Saturday it's time to eliminate the threat from Iran "once and for all" in a speech about forming a new government following a meeting earlier this week with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot.
"The Iranian regime, which seeks to destroy Israel, is once again working to revive its nuclear program," Netanyahu said, translated from Hebrew. "And let this be clear: This murderous regime, which did not hesitate to murder many thousands of its own people, will not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us."
"It will do so the moment it manages to resume uranium enrichment and the accelerated development of nuclear weapons," he continued.
Netanyahu said he met with Eisenkot on Thursday, and the meeting "only strengthened my understanding of how essential it is to establish a national unity government at this time."
In last month's election , Netanyahu's Likud party and its allies received 53 seats in the Knesset, short of the 61 needed to form a government and keep him as prime minister. Eisenkot's Yashar party and its allies won 48 seats, while the Arab coalition took 19 seats.
Netanyahu wondered aloud why Eisenkot would potentially side with the Arab coalition to form what he called a "fragile and dangerous government." Netanyahu is clinging to hopes Eisenkot will agree to a deal to establish a majority and cut out the Arab parties, who he has accused of stealing the election . On Saturday, he referred to them as "supporters of terrorism."
"We must remove this existential threat from over our heads once and for all," Netanyahu said, referring to Iran. "A narrow government, or a government that relies on supporters of terrorism, will not be able to achieve this monumental goal. But a national unity government can achieve it in time, thereby ensuring Israel's security for many years to come."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthi militant group said it intercepted and destroyed two drones on Saturday.
The drones were intercepted near Riyadh and over the southern region. The coalition was not more specific about where in the south it had been intercepted. Riyadh, the country's capital, is located in central Saudi Arabia, though hundreds of miles from the Houthis' base of operations in Yemen.
It was a busy week of drone and missile interceptions by the Saudis. The two drones intercepted on Saturday afternoon were the first since one was fired at the eastern, oil-rich region of the country on Thursday. Multiple drones in the east and near Riyadh were interrupted Thursday, while two ballistic missiles were shot down on Wednesday in the western part of Saudi Arabia and three others were shot down near Riyadh, according to the coalition.
Two drones were also intercepted on Wednesday, the coalition said, though one destroyed near Mecca was disavowed by the Houthis, who have said they will not target the holy city.
Multiple drones, ballistic missiles and cruise missiles were also intercepted over different parts of Saudi Arabia on Monday, the same day the coalition said it took out a weapons manufacturing facility in Yemen.
Iran and the United States should "immediately" allow fertilizer shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to ease the crisis in some of the most vulnerable countries, a senior U.N. official said Saturday.
Jorge Moreira da Silva, head of the U.N. Office for Project Services, told the COP31 climate talks in the Turkish resort city of Antalya that the lack of fertilizers could push millions into poverty.
While Iran and the United States are still trying to negotiate an end to the conflict, Moreira da Silva said he had the same message for both countries.
"They should continue their negotiations about the comprehensive deal — but that deal should not avoid an immediate, exceptional, limited, and time-bound solution for the fertilizers," he said.
"Basically what we need is five vessels a day with fertilizers," he added.
Before the conflict, a third of the world's fertilizers passed through the Strait of Hormuz, and since the blockades, their prices had risen by 30%, Moreira da Silva said.
Sudan's finance minister recently told him the price of food there had doubled in six months, he added. In Nepal, they told him that farmers could no longer afford to buy fertilizers.
"So it's very important that we are aware that countries such as Mozambique, Kenya, Sudan, Somalia, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka are facing very significant impact," Moreira da Silva said.
The effects of this shortage could be catastrophic, he warned.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps claims to have shot down an American MQ-1 "Predator" drone for the second straight day on Saturday.
This was the 17th MQ-1 drone shot down by Iran, according to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, though that number was not possible to verify. The U.S. certainly has lost a number of the drones, however, either to them being shot down or crashing.
The drone was shot down over Iran's Qeshm Island, which is located along the northern coast of the Strait of Hormuz. Like Friday, the strike was credited to Iran's alleged new air defense system.
The U.S. has lost dozens of unmanned aircraft during the war with Iran, according to a congressional report dated Oct. 5. Forty-five MQ-9 Reaper drones have been lost, just through mid-August, while at least three Predator drones were previously destroyed, according to the report.
There were at least 81 manned or unmanned aircraft lost during the war in Iran through early October, according to the report. As of Aug. 1, the losses amounted to a cost of between $1.9 billion and $3.3 billion.
Iran's military said on Saturday that fires had broken out on a total of three oil tankers that struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has insisted vessels obtain its authorization to cross the strait since war erupted with the United States in February, and has attacked ships that do not comply.
"A short while ago, two oil tankers that had switched off their radar and positioning systems and were secretly attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an unauthorized route exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine," the Revolutionary Guards Corps said in a statement on the incident in the south of the waterway, carried by the Iranian state broadcaster early on Saturday.
A separate statement from Iran's conventional navy said another tanker "navigating through the unsafe and prohibited zone east of the Strait of Hormuz with its tracking and identification systems switched off, caught fire and was forced to stop after striking a naval mine".
The statements did not provide the names or origins of the vessels but the Guards said one of those hit in south Hormuz was a supertanker.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Saturday that explosions rang out on two oil tankers after they struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz, where Tehran has restricted navigation.

articles.title_orig: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
articles.title_zh: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
articles.content_orig:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The US has not confirmed Zelensky's comments, which come after US President Donald Trump's envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable.
Russia controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.
He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.
Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.
Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.
It is not clear the US is actually proposing Nato membership â the White House has not yet replied to a request for comment and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees that as unrealistic.
Other Nato members are wary and the Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.
It is possible the American envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky said recently that the US mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.
Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.
So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public in order to re-open a discussion that had been considered all-but closed.
He maintains that the idea is now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security.
It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.
The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.
Russia has insisted again that it will not agree to cease fighting until a final peace deal is in place that would include handing over territories its troops have not captured, in addition to the Crimean peninsula it annexed illegally in 2014.
Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.
The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.
Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service , which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.
Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday after the G7 Foreign Ministers' meeting in Paris, that "bad things are happening to the Iranian economy and it's unfortunate."
The U.S. Air Force abruptly relocated more than a dozen aircraft from RAF Mildenhall in eastern England amid an emerging security threat, U.S. officials confirmed Tuesday.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the move, citing sources who said the threat originated in Iran.
As U.S. officials assessed the threat's nature and urgency, commanders raised the base's security level to Force Protection Condition Charlie, the military's second-highest alert level, indicating a likely terrorist threat against personnel or facilities.
IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS
U.S. Air Force KC-135, used for in-flight refueling, takes off from RAF Mildenhall Airbase. (AP Photo/Max Nash, File)
Flight-tracking data and open-source analysts with the Military Air Tracking Alliance identified 13 U.S. aircraft leaving the base late Monday, the Associated Press said.
Nine Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers were moved to airfields in Scotland, Germany and Spain.
Three CV-22B Ospreys were relocated to nearby RAF Lakenheath, which has hardened aircraft shelters.
A U.S. official told The Associated Press the moves were precautionary, noting that some aircraft were on rotational deployments while others were permanently stationed in the United Kingdom .
IRAN UNDER SCRUTINY AFTER PLOT FOILED NEAR UK BASE USED BY US MILITARY
American aircrews check a B-52 Stratofortress long-range subsonic bomber aircraft on the pan at RAF Fairford. The United Kingdom reportedly is refusing to let the United States use the base for a potential attack on Iran. (Getty Images)
The move marks the second major relocation of U.S. military aircraft from Britain in less than two months.
In early October, the Air Force pulled heavy bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire after British counterterrorism police stopped three suspicious vans headed toward the base Sept. 27.
Two men have since been charged under the United Kingdom's National Security Act.
Separately, the Justice Department unsealed indictments against three Iranian-backed operatives on Tuesday accused of involvement in coordinated terrorist plots across Europe, including RAF Fairford.
UK POLICE ARREST 'EXPLOSIVE' SUSPECTS NEAR US AIRBASE, KEY TO IRAN WAR
The main gate of RAF Fairford is pictured on September 27, 2026 in Fairford, United Kingdom. Police declared a major incident after evacuating residents from their homes in Whelford, a village about one mile from RAF Fairford, a military base that hosts U.S. Air Force bombers involved in the Iran conflict. (David Bown/Getty Images)
RAF Mildenhall is home to the 100th Air Refueling Wing, the only permanently based U.S. tanker wing in Europe.
Its KC-135 Stratotankers support allied aerial refueling and long-range strike missions across the region.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Washington routinely repositions military forces.
"We are constantly repositioning forces around the world for a variety of reasons," Rubio told reporters when asked about the evacuation.

A 10 Downing Street spokesperson said British air bases remain secure and that London and Washington continuously share intelligence on potential threats.
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

The White House said billionaire Elon Musk would accompany Mr Trump on the China visit, but a senior US official said he would not attend the talks with Mr Xi and Mr Putin.

articles.title_orig: A ‘Generational Clash’ Is Fueling Europe’s Protests
articles.title_zh: A ‘Generational Clash’ Is Fueling Europe’s Protests
articles.content_orig:
John Last is a freelance journalist and former foreign correspondent living outside Ottawa, Canada.
Across Europe, young people are being arrested in their thousands. In Milan, jackbooted soldiers from the Italian military — average age, 38 — haul protesters, some of whom are as young as 12 and 13, away from picket lines and into armored vehicles. Italy’s government — average age, 60 — has passed a new decree allowing detainments for up to 24 hours without charge. Vandals can now be arrested 48 hours after their crimes; Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, 53, has called for their parents to face financial penalties too.
Italy’s weekend of protests at the end of October, in at least a dozen major cities, was the most destructive in recent memory. In Milan, hooded youths looted the city’s luxury stores, pilfering products, one reporter wrote , “that they cannot afford and may never be able to buy.” But as shocking as Italy’s protests have been, they pale in comparison to those in France. Mobs of people have paralyzed city centers across the country for weeks. The grand streets of Paris have been blanketed in acrid smoke. French President Emmanuel Macron has accused an alliance of “radical far-left groups [and] criminals” of trying “to bring down the Republic.” Fifty-three police officers were injured over the course of a single weekend.
After more than a month, it is almost hard to believe that protests of this magnitude began over the failures of a university application portal . But by now, the grievances have multiplied: the high cost of fuel, the crowding of schools, the inaccessibility of housing, the growing precarity of work. In turn, the protests have taken on an existential desperation. An unmistakable vibe of despair permeates the masked protesters. “They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can’t say anything,” one protester in Paris told the BBC. “It’s been too long, it’s been too much.”
“They” are the elder-elite of Europe, the now-aged baby boomers who greedily gobbled up the assets of their societies: a third of Italy’s housing stock; a quarter of France’s public spending; 98% of the average Spanish worker’s salary, in the form of monthly rent. While young people reel from crisis to crisis — wars, economic stagnation, climate disaster, a pandemic — they cash in. Rising prices, precarious work, broken schools: As a generation, the boomers have remained largely unaffected while the value of their real estate and investments boomed. As their wealth and number grew, they came to set the agendas of unions, politicians and the media, and they bent the state to suppress any who would rally against them. They pioneered a playbook to extract the last cents of value from Europe’s bloated and aging welfare states before departing a world they leave on the threshold of self-destruction.
But the underclass in their wake cannot be restrained forever. In the spasms across Europe, we are witnessing a generational uprising, a war on the reckless landlordism of the last propertied generation. They gouged too deep and for too long; like the dwarves of Moria, they accidentally unleashed a primal foe. “It has been called the children’s war,” La Repubblica reports : an insurgency against calcifying Western gerontocracies waged by their own offspring.
In some ways, generational inequality is felt before it can be measured. It is usually assumed that people naturally accumulate wealth over their lifetime, and that a person in their ‘70s should own more in assets than a relatively new worker in their ‘30s. But it wasn’t always so. Today’s old-age security is the result of a general crisis of elder poverty that proliferated across the Western world in the 1920s and ‘30s when people still literally worked themselves to death, or else died penniless. To solve this problem, states embraced a system of “asymmetric socialization,” according to Pieter Vanhuysse, a leading expert in political demography at the University of Southern Denmark. In short, the state took care of the elderly while the family was still mostly expected to take care of the young.
Today, it is hard to imagine a crisis of elder poverty on a similar scale to that of the 1930s, not least because the elderly account for such a large percentage of the population. In France and Italy, thanks to longer lifespans and low rates of reproduction, the number of citizens over 65 has doubled since the arrival of the boomer generation, born between 1946 and 1964, to one in five and one in four residents, respectively. Nor is the phenomenon limited to Europe. In the United States, where fertility rates are higher, the median age has risen by 10 years since 1960. There are fewer than a billion seniors in the world today; by 2060, that number is expected to double and account for a fifth of global population.
As seniors have exploded in number, they have exercised an ever-greater influence on politics. In France, the United Kingdom, Germany, the U.S. and many other developed nations, those aged 65 and over are between 10% and 20% more likely to vote than those aged 18-25. This has contributed to a shocking representative gap — people under 30 account for half of the world’s population but just 2% of its legislators. “There’s a clear representational deficit,” said Daniel Stockemer, a political scientist at the University of Ottawa. “It creates a problem that youth’s concerns are not taken sufficiently into consideration, that youth are not sufficiently included in decision-making processes.”
In a study of intergenerational fairness in state spending, Vanhuysse found a disproportionate favoritism toward the old in nearly all the countries surveyed. Nearly a quarter of young Europeans and nearly half of young Americans are struggling financially; they will also disproportionately bear the weight of the ecological destruction and public debt accumulated by the boomers.
France, where youth first took to the streets, is among the worst offenders. There, public debt now exceeds the value of its economy. In Vanhuysse’s index, it ranks just behind Japan for the disproportionate political power it grants the elderly — nearly two in five civil servants are over 50 , a number that has rapidly increased since 2011. Vanhuysse estimates roughly $5 is spent on elderly citizens for every $1 spent on youth. That is clearly evident in the crumbling, overcrowded schools and inadequate universities that first spurred young people onto the streets. State pensions, meanwhile, eat up a quarter of the country’s public spending — including a whole third of the education ministry’s budget.
All of this would not be so galling if it were not for the fact that the generation now draining state coffers already benefited from an unprecedented golden age of growth. Boomers entered the workforce at the peak of unionization and enjoyed stable employment, wages that beat inflation and guaranteed pensions upon retirement. They were buying starter homes when housing could be had for just two or three years’ income. Today it is nearly 10 .
Boomers used this unprecedented growth to acquire assets well beyond their needs, sitting on valuable housing stock — 28% of family homes in the U.S., for example — desperately desired by the next generation. Then they leveraged those assets to squeeze younger generations. In Australia, seniors’ investment in rental properties has increased 1,500% at the same time as rents have nearly doubled. Where boomers were able to buy property cheaply and grow their money in investments, young people today spend a vast percentage of their earnings on rent — which, more often than not, is passive income for elderly landlords.
The result is a generation that feels it has been actively held back from achieving the same or better lives than their parents had by that same generation’s relentless extraction of money. Today, Vanhuysse found, a working person in France can expect their lifetime wealth to be

articles.title_orig: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
articles.title_zh: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
articles.content_orig:
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta €805m (£670m; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.
Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.
It has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.
The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.
A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it planned to appeal.
The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.
Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery.
The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".
It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation".
Meta told the BBC: "We strongly disagree with the [regulator's] assessment of the facts, its application of the law, and the disproportionate level of the fine.
"This is a straightforward feature which helps people post photos and videos to Facebook. People must give permission on their device before it can operate, and they can change this permission at any time via their settings."
Last month, Meta, which is also behind Instagram and WhatsApp, was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.
A US judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

articles.title_orig: Middle East monarchies brace for Trump corruption scrutiny after blue wave
articles.title_zh: Middle East monarchies brace for Trump corruption scrutiny after blue wave
articles.content_orig:
The US elections have opened a new chapter for artificial intelligence investments by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, democratic gains in Congress, potential restrictions on access to advanced chips, and criticism of data center expansion could alter the conditions under which both countries develop their technology projects.
The Gulf’s bid to become a global leader in computing depends largely on American technology. Therefore, political changes in Washington are raising concerns about the supply of semiconductors, partnerships with technology companies, and the construction of large-scale computing facilities.
Added to this is the debate over the electricity and water consumption of data centers in the United States, this situation could favor the expansion of technological infrastructure in the Middle East, although it also leaves the Gulf countries exposed to regulatory decisions from Washington.
The Democratic victory in the midterm elections introduces new elements to the technological relationship between Washington, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. When the party assumes control of Congress in January, it will have greater opportunities to oversee the artificial intelligence industry. Among the issues that could occupy the legislative agenda are international technological alliances, export controls, and access to advanced computing systems.
This concern is also reflected at the state level, with Democratic candidates who support limiting large data centers winning the governorships of Texas and Georgia. Part of this opposition stems from the impact data centers have on local resources, particularly the increased cost of electricity and water consumption, both of which are gaining traction in discussions about approving new projects.
If these restrictions gain strength, some technology companies could find it more difficult to expand their facilities in the United States and consider other markets to develop their infrastructure.
The supply of semiconductors is one of the most sensitive issues for artificial intelligence projects in the Gulf. Building data centers requires advanced processors, servers, and computing power that depends on international manufacturers and suppliers. Angeline Ong, senior technical analyst at IG, points out that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are seeking to position themselves as global computing hubs for AI, however, access to much of the necessary technology remains contingent on decisions made in Washington.
US restrictions on advanced chips therefore represent a factor that could limit the technological autonomy of regional operators. Adding to this situation is a condition that Nvidia has reportedly set for its data center clients worldwide: at least 51 % of its services must be allocated to non-Chinese companies, according to information published by the Financial Times.
The same outlet reported that Oracle canceled a $7 billion chip leasing agreement with the Chinese company Tencent after receiving pressure from Washington. These cases show that the development of infrastructure for artificial intelligence does not depend solely on investment and the availability of equipment, trade relationships and geopolitical decisions can also determine who has access to this technology and under what conditions.
Despite the restrictions, the main artificial intelligence projects in the Gulf maintain agreements with major US companies, in Saudi Arabia, Humain has the backing of the Public Investment Fund and Saudi Aramco, and the company has established alliances with Amazon Web Services Nvidia and Microsoft to develop its technological capabilities.
In the United Arab Emirates, Microsoft invested $1.5 billion in G42, a technology group based in Abu Dhabi. Through its subsidiary Core42, the company develops cloud infrastructure services and computing solutions for artificial intelligence. According to Angeline Ong, the 51% requirement should not pose an immediate problem for Humain or G42/Core42, as both maintain partner networks oriented toward the West.
Sam Winter-Levy of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace also believes the immediate impact on G42 and Core42 would be limited. However, their current US authorizations expire in April 2027, unless renewed or replaced. This date adds pressure for both companies to maintain operations within the conditions set by Washington. This is compounded by existing delays in deliveries of approved advanced chips due to regulatory hurdles and concerns about potential Chinese access to this technology.
The Humain case presents another element that deserves attention. The company has used technology from MiniMax, a Chinese developer of artificial intelligence models. For now, it is unclear whether the use of Chinese models to provide services to clients in other countries would count toward the limit set by Nvidia.
Winter-Levy explains that Gulf companies have more freedom to decide which AI models to develop or use than to choose the infrastructure needed to run them. The difference is significant. The models are systems trained to perform specific tasks, while their operation depends on a physical infrastructure made up of chips, servers, and specialized equipment.
This means that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates can explore different alternatives for developing their artificial intelligence models, but they have fewer options when they need access to next-generation processors. In this context, diversifying semiconductor suppliers and developing their own manufacturing capabilities are among the alternatives for reducing technological dependence.
The difficulties in expanding large IT facilities within the United States could also benefit the Middle East. Neil Quilliam, a specialist on the region at Chatham House, points out that Gulf governments can more easily offer land, energy supplies, and favorable regulatory conditions than some US jurisdictions.
This environment could prove attractive to technology companies that need to expand their processing capacity and are looking for new locations for their data centers. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates thus have the opportunity to attract new investment and consolidate their digital infrastructures.
However, having available land and energy does not equate to technological independence. Access to advanced semiconductors and the conditions for their use still depend on decisions made outside the region. Quilliam warns that facilitating access to US chips does not mean Washington will relinquish control over their use. The fundamental question remains: who can use this technology and who reaps the benefits of its development?
The new political balance in the United States could expand oversight of international technology agreements. Democrats will have the power to investigate partnerships, hold hearings, and promote measures related to data centers and export controls. However, a breakdown in cooperation with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates is not an inevitable scenario.
Quilliam believes there is bipartisan support for keeping Gulf countries within the US technology ecosystem, rather than favoring closer ties with Chinese suppliers. The extent of any potential restrictions will depend on the decisions Washington makes and the conditions it sets for the supply and use of advanced technology Saudi Arabia and for the United Arab Emirates, the challenge lies in expanding their artificial intelligence capabilities without relying excessively on external regulatory changes.
The expansion of data centers can strengthen their presence in the global digital economy, but access to semiconductors will remain crucial for the development of their technology projects.

articles.title_orig: Why homeowners who go electric have a secret advantage
articles.title_zh: Why homeowners who go electric have a secret advantage
articles.content_orig:
Illustrative photo. Source: Julian Herzog ( Website ) / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.
About 6% of U.S. households with at least one vehicle owned an all-electric or plug-in hybrid in 2025, the first year the Census Bureau asked about EV ownership.
EV ownership is most concentrated in the West and major metropolitan areas, according to an Axios analysis of newly released Census Bureau data.
This is reported by Axios .
Where EVs are taking hold will shape who benefits first from electric transportation, where charging networks expand and how quickly the country’s auto market shifts away from gas-powered cars.
California had the highest share of households with an all-electric or plug-in hybrid vehicle in 2025, at 15% - more than double the national rate. Washington, at 9.6%, and Hawaii, at 9.1%, followed, then Nevada at 8.8% and Vermont at 8.1%. North Dakota (1.4%), Wyoming (1.7%) and Louisiana (1.8%) were among the states with the lowest shares.
California’s lead reflects decades of policies encouraging EV purchases and requiring automakers to offer electric models. The state began adopting zero-emission vehicle requirements in 1990. In 2025, California accounted for nearly 30% of U.S. zero-emission passenger vehicle sales, despite having 12% of the nation’s population.
EV ownership was especially concentrated in major metropolitan areas. In the Austin metro area, the share was 9.3%, more than double Texas’s statewide rate of 4.5%. San Francisco’s share was 20%, a high figure in California.
Research has linked higher EV adoption around population centers to household income. Another study found that establishing charging infrastructure boosts adoption, particularly in higher-income areas.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia board urged to consider 'potential return of Jensen Huang' by two major investors
articles.title_zh: Nvidia board urged to consider 'potential return of Jensen Huang' by two major investors
articles.content_orig:
Two major Nvidia shareholders are calling on the board of directors to weigh all options for the company's future leadership, including "the potential return of Jensen Huang."
Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner posted a letter on X on Friday that urges Nvidia's board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia." The letter is also signed by Atreides Management's Gavin Baker.
Nvidia was Altimeter Capital's largest disclosed equity holding in its most recent SEC filing , with a 9.4 million-share stake worth nearly $1.9 billion as of June 30. Atreides held 1.2 million shares worth nearly $250 million at the end of June.
The letter said Nvidia will be "capably led" by interim CEO Colette Kress , who served as Nvidia's CFO for 13 years before the board announced Thursday that she'd lead the company in Huang's absence.
"But the Founder and long time incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known," the letter concludes. The document did not call for Huang's immediate reinstatement.
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday amid multiple affair allegations, including one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang , who also worked with Nvidia customer Megaspeed . The Singapore-based company is being investigated by the Justice Department for possibly redirecting some of its supply of Nvidia's restricted artificial intelligence chips to China.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X Friday that he signed a petition asking to reinstate Huang. A petition circulating online called "Stand with Jensen" claims to have more than 100,000 signatures, including more than 5,000 current Nvidia employees.
Musk said on X Saturday that without Huang, some "critical deals will be lost."
Another letter sent Friday called on U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick to testify about Megaspeed before the House Intelligence Committee.
Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10 about whether the Commerce Department is "properly performing its broader role of preventing China from acquiring advanced AI chips," according to the letter. Huang has also been asked to testify .
The Commerce Department originally launched an investigation into Megaspeed that was moved to the Justice Department in 2025 after Nvidia's lawyer contacted a senior Commerce official, according to The New York Times.
President Donald Trump is scheduled to visit China on Thursday, but doesn't plan to raise Nvidia and the suspected spy affair during his meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping , according to U.S. officials. Musk is expected to join Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.

articles.title_orig: With shifting Iran rhetoric following US elections, Trump leaves Mideast in limbo about path ahead
articles.title_zh: With shifting Iran rhetoric following US elections, Trump leaves Mideast in limbo about path ahead
articles.content_orig:
After President Trump's midterm election losses and Israel's ongoing political shakeup, Gulf countries are stuck in limbo as Trump's options to end the war in Iran dwindle.
The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran is in its ninth month, and President Trump is confronting new realities that leave him with dwindling options to ending the conflict. Republicans just lost their majority in Congress, in part because of the unpopular war with Iran and its downstream consequences, like high gas prices. And Trump's wartime ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is on the cusp of losing power after elections there. Joining us to talk about where things go from here is NPR's correspondent in Dubai, Aya Batrawy. Aya, good morning.
AYA BATRAWY, BYLINE: Good morning, Michel.
MARTIN: Have you seen a shift in Trump's policy on Iran now after these election losses, or at least a shift in tone?
BATRAWY: There has been a shift in rhetoric since the midterms. So before this blue wave, his administration had been warning Gulf allies like Saudi Arabia to prepare for another major U.S. attack on Iran. And Trump was publicly threatening to do that, saying he could finish the job with quick, intense strikes. But then this week, Trump stuck (ph) a different tone after he met mediator Qatar's prime minister at the White House. After that, Trump said, at this point, attacks on Iran seem unlikely. He said Gulf Arab allies actually prefer the status quo, and that's true. The UAE and others are really worried about Iran's counterstrikes. You know, these wealthy Gulf Arab countries, Michel - they have been plunged into economic recession because of the war.
But also, Trump had these election losses in the U.S., and Israel's in the midst of its own political shakeup. So with limited options, he's trying to focus on domestic problems and keep things as they are with Iran. That means economic pressure, like sanctions and the U.S. naval blockade on Iran to starve them of oil exports. And just this week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran is feeling the pain of this policy because, he says, quote, "eventually you have to eat."
MARTIN: So what does keeping the status quo actually look like in the Gulf? And is that even tenable?
BATRAWY: Well, both sides have their finger on the trigger, and fighting can resume at any moment. So this leaves the region suspended in uncertainty. The U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier with thousands of troops to the region. And just today, Iran says the U.S. again struck an island in the Strait of Hormuz, an area Iran has drones and radars in. And Iran says it hit back, targeting a U.S. radar in Bahrain. So status quo means Iran keeps hitting ships in the Strait of Hormuz. There are huge areas now along the UAE's coastline that are actually closed because of oil spills. And then you have Arab partners that still can't get, you know, using their ports for imports or exports like before. And there's a war raging between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen, which was reignited in part because of this open-ended Iran conflict.
MARTIN: Are there signs that the U.S. and Iran could even sit down again for direct talks?
BATRAWY: So Iran's been saying it's willing to halt attacks on oil tankers for a short period, and they want a U.S. response to that offer. But they also have listed seven demands that they want met before talks on their nuclear program can even begin. Rubio says the demands are unrealistic and absurd. They include the U.S. unfreezing billions of Iran's dollars in overseas banks and ending sanctions and the naval blockade. I spoke with Hasan Alhasan. He's a senior fellow from Bahrain with the International Institute for Strategic Studies, and he says Iran is more defiant.
HASAN ALHASAN: The war has confirmed and validated the views of hard-liners in Iran that were always skeptical of diplomatic engagement. So I think, if anything, the war has made Iran arguably more threatening. It's now no longer deterred by the possibility, the threat, of a U.S. or Israeli assault because that has happened.
BATRAWY: So with Iran arguably more threatening, you have just yesterday Trump writing on Truth Social that the U.S. itself doesn't need a deal with Iran - he says because, in his words, "we've got their money."
MARTIN: That is NPR's Aya Batrawy in Dubai. Thanks, Aya.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin plan unprecedented joint meeting on APEC sidelines, White House and Kremlin say
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin plan unprecedented joint meeting on APEC sidelines, White House and Kremlin say
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump will meet jointly next week with China’s leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the White House said Friday, a first-ever trilateral sit-down between the leaders of the three countries.
The meeting, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, will focus on nuclear non-proliferation, a topic Trump has said he believes could yield a new agreement between the world’s biggest nuclear-armed states.
“The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesman, told reporters.
The Kremlin says that the meeting will take place on November 19 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, but there has been no confirmation yet from China.
While a trilateral convention taking this exact formation is unprecedented, separately the leaders have a wealth of history.
Since becoming president in 2013, Xi has met with Putin dozens of times. The pair have built a close alliance, bound by ties that run deep between their nations.
China has claimed neutrality in the war and sought to position itself as a potential peace broker. But NATO allies believe it has been instrumental in Russia’s effort to defeat Ukraine, providing Moscow with equipment to support weapon assembly, and contributing technology and imagery.
Trump and Putin have convened in-person on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in 2025. The two leaders’ relationship has, at times, been tumultuous, but it appears to have strengthened in recent months.
Trump faced a barrage of domestic criticism in October when he suspended fuel export sanctions on Russia for at least six months, allowing Putin to release diesel into the global energy market at a time when US fuel prices were skyrocketing.
A bipartisan group of lawmakers accused Trump of defying a federal law designed to crack down on Russia and stifle its economy amid its war on Ukraine.
The last nuclear arms treaty between the US and Russia expired in February.
China, meanwhile, has been rapidly building its nuclear arsenal.
Officials downplayed the prospect of striking a new deal on nuclear matters, suggesting instead the talks would be a starting point.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior US official said. “I would characterize this as the entry point, the first conversation, certainly at the leader level, between these countries.”
“So this is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward,” the official went on.
While officials said the three leaders also planned to discuss Iran, it is unclear if they intend to discuss Russia’s near-five-year-old conflict with Ukraine.
Back in October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky voiced concern that a trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin might lead to dealmaking about the future of Ukraine without consulting Kyiv.
“We really don’t want this to turn into ‘Yalta 2, 3, 4,’ with a redistribution of influence,” Zelensky told journalists last month, drawing a comparison with the 1945 Yalta Conference in Crimea at which the Allied powers effectively redrew the global map in the aftermath of World War Two.
A senior US official said Elon Musk was expected to go on the trip with Trump, among others, though he is not expected to attend the trilateral meeting.

articles.title_orig: Brain Implants Give A.L.S. Patients the Voice to Speak and Sing
articles.title_zh: Brain Implants Give A.L.S. Patients the Voice to Speak and Sing
articles.content_orig:
Telepathy, the ability to communicate thoughts directly from one mind to another, is such a beautiful emotional connection between humans. It has long been a feature of science fiction, however, advances in neuroscience and artificial intelligence are bringing a restrained version of this idea closer to reality through brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). BCIs help to translate patterns of brain activity into commands, text or speech, hence allowing communication without physically speaking. Unlike fictional telepathy, the actual technology is composed of electrodes, computer algorithms and precisely trained systems. The key question is whether decoding intended words could eventually lead to direct thought-based communication.
“The human brain is made up of billions of neurons that talk through electrical and chemical signals”. Let’s look at how a BCI works: When a person intends to speak, move or perform an action, groups of neurons produce patterns of activity that can be recorded.  Electrodes are used to capture these signals, and in the meanwhile the machine-learning algorithms identify patterns associated with particular words or intended movements. The information is then decoded and can be displayed as a text on a screen, control a computer cursor or be converted into synthetic speech. There are two kinds of BCIs: Invasive BCIs, which are implanted in the brain to record detailed signals, and non-invasive BCIs, which record activity from outside the skull, with different levels of precision.
“The human brain is made up of billions of neurons that talk through electrical and chemical signals.”
A study published in Nature Medicine in June 2026 showed long-term, independent use of a BCI by a man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a degenerative motor neuron disease. Researchers implanted small electrode arrays in his brain to record neural activity, and the system translated his attempted speech into text, giving him cursor control over a computer. Over nearly two years, he used the system at home for more than 3,800 hours, communicating 183,060 sentences (almost 2 million words) at an average rate of 56 words per minute. This suggested that BCI could support everyday tasks like internet browsing and continued employment, rather than being functional only during supervised laboratory experiments. However, with only one participant, it remains unclear whether the results generalise without further scientific studies.
Text can communicate a message, but it cannot fully capture the emotion, personality or tone behind it. In 2025, a group of researchers built a brain-to-voice system that converted neural activity into audible speech in real time for a man with ALS. It’s fascinating how the system could recreate a voice resembling his voice before illness and allowed him to change his intonation, emphasise words and even sing short melodies. This is an important milestone because communication is not simply about conveying information but also expressing human emotions like humour, excitement and uncertainty. Such technology could help people who have lost their innate speech express in a way that feels more personal.
“Text can communicate a message, but it cannot fully capture the emotion, personality or tone behind it.”
The next step towards telepathy would be communicating through inner speech i.e. the voice we experience in our minds when we think in our mother tongue and want to speak in a different language, read silently or mentally rehearse a conversation. Studies suggest that some of these imagined words can be decoded from brain activity under controlled conditions. However, thoughts are not always expressed in a language. We can think through memories, images or vague ideas without forming a clear sentence. This makes interpreting inner speech different from accessing every thought in someone’s mind. A system that identifies an intended sentence is not necessarily able to recognise everything a person thinks.
“The next step towards telepathy would be communicating through inner speech.”
Imagine being able to send a message to someone simply by aiming to say it, without reaching for a phone or speaking aloud. A future BCI might translate that intended message into digital information and transmit it to another person’s device, making communication faster. However, this would still be technology-mediated interaction rather than a direct connection between two brains.
The challenges that come along cannot be ignored. Advanced implanted BCIs require brain surgery, which carries risks and makes large-scale use more complex. The prospect of decoding intended words raises significant questions about mental privacy: who controls neural data, and how can people ensure that private thoughts remain private? Hence, clear consent, strong data protection and deliberate user activation would be imperative as these technologies develop. Scientific progress must therefore be measured not only by how much information a system can decode, but how safely and independently can people utilise it.
“W ho controls neural data, and how can people ensure that private thoughts remain private?”
This raises the question: Are we approaching telepathy? The boundary between science fiction and scientific reality is becoming less clear, but the gap between decoding a message and understanding a mind remains enormous. Human thoughts are deeply personal and often messy, unspoken and difficult to put into words. Decoding them consistently with precision is a far more intricate challenge than simply recognising a sentence. Perhaps the real question is not whether technology will allow us to read minds, but how much control we should have over what our minds reveal. As BCIs continue to evolve, they could change not only how humans communicate, but also how we define privacy, expression and the relationship between the brain and technology.

articles.title_orig: Bitcoin price analysis: BTC continues to decline Saturday, entering 'deep value zone'
articles.title_zh: Bitcoin price analysis: BTC continues to decline Saturday, entering 'deep value zone'
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Bitcoin sits 47% below its October 2025 record, and past cycles fell 70% to 82% one year after peaking, so deeper losses remain possible.
Spot Bitcoin ETFs have bled money since October, with the last three sessions all posting outflows as cumulative inflows dropped from $58 billion to $55 billion.
Goldman Sachs added another Fed rate hike to its outlook after hot inflation data, while the 10-year Treasury yield hit 5% and competes with Bitcoin.
It sounds nuts, but SoFi is giving new Active Invest users up to $1,000 in stock for a limited time, and all it takes is a $50 deposit to get started. See for yourself (Sponsor)
Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) traded at $66,485 on Saturday morning, November 14. That is 3.96% lower in 24 hours and 12.26% lower over seven days. Earlier in the week it was still above $70,000. As recently as October 21, it closed at $84,082.27.
Holders keep coming back to one recovery number: the September rally high of $87,397. If Bitcoin can get back there, the 2026 rebound held. History points the other way. One year after its 2013, 2017 and 2021 peaks, Bitcoin was down about 70%, 82% and 75%, according to a CoinDesk cycle comparison.
So the question is whether Bitcoin can reclaim $87,397 in 2027, or whether this decline still has further to fall.
At today's price, Bitcoin's market cap (price multiplied by coins in circulation) is about $1.34 trillion. It is still the No. 1 crypto asset. The coin sits 47.27% below the record of $126,080, set on October 6, 2025. It is down 29.85% over the past year and 24.08% year to date.
SoFi Active Invest is offering a limited-time promotion. Open an account, fund it with $50 or more, and you could receive up to $1,000 in complimentary stock for Active Invest accounts. See for yourself by clicking here now. (Sponsor)
The climb is harder than the chart suggests because of supply dilution. Miners create new bitcoin with every block they add, so the circulating supply keeps growing. Bitcoin is up just 4.11% from $63,857.77 five years ago. The network is worth more today than it was at that price, because more coins exist. The same logic applies going forward. Every return to an old price level takes more new dollars than the previous visit did.
This cycle has been softer than past ones so far. A one-year loss of about 30% is a long way from 70% or more. But 2022 shows that the first flush is often not the last. Bitcoin hit a June 2022 low of $17,697.70 and then broke lower to $15,598.50 in November. This year already produced a June closing low of $58,566.09. Riding a mania on the way up is one skill; knowing when to step aside is another, and we wrote a free handbook on both halves of that trade.
Spot Bitcoin ETFs are funds that hold actual bitcoin and trade like stocks. Their cumulative net inflow, meaning all the money that has come in minus all the money that has gone out, peaked at $57.96 billion on October 21. By November 13 it had dropped to $54.63 billion. Total net assets fell from $109.31 billion to $86.20 billion over the same period. The last three sessions all lost money: $299.90 million, $284.00 million and $185.45 million. The worst day was October 30, with $643.33 million in outflows.
Flows have moved the price before. Inflows of $526.60 million on October 19 and $528.40 million on October 21 came right before the 30-day high that same week. We covered how fast that reversed in our October look at ETF outflows.
The 10-year Treasury yield reached 5.10% on November 12, up from 4.84% on November 5. The Fed's target rate has an upper limit of 4.00%, unchanged over the past month. Goldman Sachs ( NYSE:GS ) added another rate hike to its Fed outlook after hot inflation data. When a government bond pays 5% with no risk, an asset that pays no yield, like Bitcoin, has to compete for that money. Liquidity has kept growing all the same: M2, a broad measure of money in the economy, was up 5.7% year over year as of September. That money is going somewhere other than Bitcoin.
A liquidation is when an exchange force-closes a borrowed position because the trader's collateral has run out. On November 13, CoinDesk reported about $1.64 billion in crypto futures liquidations over 24 hours, most of them long positions (trades that profit when prices rise). Prediction markets are pricing more damage. On Kalshi, traders see a 23% chance that Bitcoin falls below $55,000 before January 1, 2027, and a 15% chance it falls below $50,000. They give it a 4% chance of exceeding $100,000 by year-end.
Bitcoin has a low chance of getting back to $87,397 in 2027 unless three things happen in this order. First, ETF flows need to stay positive long enough to push cumulative inflows back above $57.96 billion. Second, the 10-year yield needs to fall back toward its early-November low of 4.84%. Third, the price needs to recover its 200-day moving average (the average closing price over the past 200 days) of $73,043.04, then its 50-day average of $80,558.31. Until Bitcoin closes above $73,043, $87,397 is not a realistic target.
If flows stay negative and yields hold above 5%, the June closing low of $58,566.09 is the level to watch. Closing below it on a daily basis would put Bitcoin on the same path as 2022, where the second low came in below the first. Keep an eye on two triggers: settling above $73,043 means the recovery case is back, and a close below $58,566 means the worst is still ahead.

articles.title_orig: Live updates: SpaceX Starship soars in orbit, still aiming for ship catch in unprecedented test flight
articles.title_zh: Live updates: SpaceX Starship soars in orbit, still aiming for ship catch in unprecedented test flight
articles.content_orig:
In a key test flight on Friday, SpaceX tried but failed to recover both stages of its massive Starship rocket.
The rocket lifted off from the company's South Texas launch facility at 4:47 p.m. local time, or 5:47 p.m. ET. SpaceX had to abort its plans to catch and reuse the booster, instead diverting it to splash into the Gulf of Mexico, where it burst into flames.
Test Flight 15, the most ambitious Starship mission to date, was the first time Elon Musk's company attempted to catch both the booster and upper stage, or spacecraft portion, of the massive rocket.
Earlier on Friday, SpaceX obtained authorization from the Federal Aviation Administration. Hours later, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop after reporting communication problems affecting "multiple" air traffic control centers. The SpaceX license wasn't effected by the flight stoppage, a spokesperson for the FAA told CNBC.
The upper stage of the Starship continued its trajectory into orbit after the company failed to catch and salvage the booster. The rocket is expected to fly around the Earth fourteen times in total. If successful, SpaceX will land the upper stage back at its Starbase facility on Saturday.
Starship's success is critical to SpaceX and its ambitions to eventually lift cargo and people to the surface of the Moon and Mars. In the near-term, SpaceX needs to send more satellites into orbit to expands its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center.
The company's constellation already includes over 11,000 active satellites in low Earth orbit. One Starship rocket has the capacity to carry up to 60 Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, the company has said, representing about 20 times the capacity of earlier Falcon 9 rockets.
In the previous Starship test flight, the company released 26 v3 satellites, and released another 26 in the Friday test flight, with the goal of "Starlink becoming 51% of the internet," SpaceX said in a post on X.
When it comes to launches, "SpaceX is likely a full decade ahead of peers on this front," William Blair analysts wrote in a note out on Friday. "Even if tonight's catch is unsuccessful, a delay by a few months is not that consequential."
Meanwhile, SpaceX is facing fresh criticism over restrictions imposed on its Starshield satellite internet service in Ukraine. Starshield is built on Starlink technology and is the military-tier of SpaceX's satellite internet service.
Earlier this week, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country's military forces had experienced limits on Starshield without warning again, harming their ability to defend against Russia's ongoing aerial attacks. Similar limits on Starshield in Ukraine were temporarily imposed last month .
Some U.S. senators have condemned the restrictions, and urged Congress to investigate SpaceX .

articles.title_orig: Pope’s visit to hub of Afro-Peruvian community casts spotlight on African slave trade to Peru
articles.title_zh: Pope’s visit to hub of Afro-Peruvian community casts spotlight on African slave trade to Peru
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV has called for an end to the violence gripping Peru, urging people not to respond to injustice with brutality, as he visited communities he once served as bishop.
“We feel threatened by the uncertainty of widespread violence and by the unspeakable suffering that continues to afflict so many of our brothers and sisters, he said, speaking at his former cathedral in Chiclayo.
Peru’s homicide rate has nearly doubled over the past five years, from 5.8 to 10.7 per 100,000 people. Reported extortion cases rose from 2,421 in 2019 to 26,734 in 2025, according to official figures cited by The Associated Press.
Security was a top concern for Peruvians in the last election. Conservative President Keiko Jujimori took office in July after promising to tackle crime. She has since declared states of emergency, including in Lima in August, then in September in prisons holding inmates linked to criminal organisations.
She has also pursued closer ties with Washington, bringing Peru into the ‘Shield of the Americas,’ a US-led regional coalition formed to carry out joint military operations against drug cartels.
Later on Saturday, in the Andean town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba with a population of about 6,000, about 20,000 people came to an outdoor Mass, where Leo also addressed violence in society.
“Selfishness, injustice and evil are not overcome by brutality, but by prayer, patience and perseverance in denouncing what is wrong, by making our pleas with determination and working diligently to bring about the necessary changes,” said the leader of the Roman Catholic church.
He also drew attention to the suffering of rural communities he used to serve, where migration and declining birth rates are emptying villages.
“Let us think, for example, of the suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future for themselves and their families in the great coastal cities,” he said.
Originally from Chicago in the United States and formerly known as Robert Francis Prevost, Leo arrived in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba by helicopter and was welcomed by a local band singing “Pope Leo, welcome home.”
He’d made the journey to the remote area many times before during his time as bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, driving himself along winding mountain roads in a pick-up truck.
The pope, who holds both US and Peruvian citizenship, spent about two decades working in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop.

articles.title_orig: AT&T begins shutting down landline services in Middle Tennessee this weekend, here's what to know
articles.title_zh: AT&T begins shutting down landline services in Middle Tennessee this weekend, here's what to know
articles.content_orig:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WTVF) — Starting this Sunday, AT&T will begin shutting down landline services across several Middle Tennessee communities after receiving permission from the Federal Communications Commission.
While the change may not affect everyone directly, experts say homeowners and business owners should know a few key things before the service disappears.
You're talking about fax lines, security lines, elevator lines — especially when it comes to condos, townhomes, business centers, medical plazas. That's where you're going to see the vast majority of them," said Stephen Burton from One Call Technology in Franklin.
The team at One Call Technology is already helping businesses prepare for the day their phone provider pulls the plug — a day that is quickly approaching.
"Different carriers are shutting off at different times, but people don't think it applies to them necessarily yet," said Burton.
An AT&T filing with the FCC shows the company plans to begin discontinuing service this weekend from dozens of wire centers across Tennessee. AT&T has until 2029 to complete the full transition.
For anyone with safety systems like fire alarms and emergency phones, experts say it's time to act now—before those systems stop working.
Navigating the changes does not have to be overwhelming.
"Reach out to a company. There are a lot in the Middle Tennessee area that you can talk with who are well aware of what's going on and can hold your hand and walk you through it," said Burton.
Something else to keep an eye on is what you're paying for older services going forward.
With pricing regulations no longer in place, some customers have seen the cost of their copper-based services climb dramatically.

articles.title_orig: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
articles.title_zh: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
articles.content_orig:
A masked demonstrator prepares to throw a Molotov cocktail as police use a water cannon to disperse students protesting education policies, rising living costs and reduced sentences for people convicted of sexual offenses against minors in Santiago, Chile, Nov. 5, 2026. Esteban Felix/AP hide caption
SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.
José Antonio Kast, a politician who spent a career railing against progressive issues, reproductive rights and welfare policies from the extreme fringes of right-wing politics, now finds himself with just 24% approval in the polls.
It is less than a year since Kast stormed to the presidency in December 2025 by avoiding all mention of his hardline stances on social matters, focusing instead on two hot-button issues whipped up in the national media: illegal immigration and public security.
But rather than pressing ahead with those at the top of his agenda, he has floundered. And as elsewhere around the Americas and worldwide, rising costs of living have come to hit him hard.
"Our salaries are maybe 20% of a European income, but with a similar cost of living – it's terrible," said Simón Echavarría, a 30-year-old architect, at a march in Santiago on Friday evening.
"We want to protest against the measures that have set us back on environmental issues, on human rights, even reducing the sentences of pedophiles – they are implementing things that nobody asked for," he said.
Behind him, heavily armed police blocked the streets and fired water cannons at protesters chanting and waving flags in the square.
Much of the recent ire stems from the revelation last month that Kast's government had signed decrees to cut the sentences of 56 prisoners whose crimes range from the rape of children to dictatorship-era human rights violations.
Kast has since admitted that this was an "error", but came out in support of the undersecretary who signed the decrees nonetheless.
But beneath the more egregious moves Kast has made in his first year in power is simmering discontent over affordability.
In July, Kast's government chose not to apply an anti-inflation tool available to the Chilean state to ease the rise in fuel prices brought about by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Protests exploded as prices shot up overnight and motorists joined long queues at gas stations to fill their tanks before the rise came into effect.
Trucks are parked along a road as drivers protest rising fuel prices and operating costs on the outskirts of Santiago, Chile, Nov. 12, 2026. Esteban Felix/AP hide caption
This week, Chile's formidable truckers' unions blockaded two major highways in an effort to exert pressure on the government and address high fuel prices.
On Friday, the strike was broken after the government backed down, sending a bill to Chile's congress which will reverse planned fuel price rises.
It is expected to be approved this month, but public anger continues to grow over the cost of living.
Politicians across the Americas who have enthusiastically aligned themselves with President Donald Trump are facing challenges similar to those confronting the U.S. administration, as rising fuel prices and the cost of everyday goods fuel public discontent.
In Argentina, far-right libertarian Javier Milei faces reelection in less than a year, with 60% of the country disapproving of his leadership amid spiraling inflation. In Peru, President Keiko Fujimori is also facing growing discontent, with 53% disapproving of her government, according to a recent Ipsos poll.
At the march in Santiago on Friday, 30-year-old veterinarian Patricia Pereira said that she was concerned about cuts to science funding, but that her discontent ran deeper.
"Here in Chile, it was a hard-won victory for children to have free education, achieved through protests, and now even that's also being called into question," she said.
Protests are likely to grow in Santiago if the government fails to address the rising cost of living. President Kast has shown little sign of doing so.
To the contrary, his budget proposal is making its way through Congress, with the government seeking cuts to education, culture, science and a host of social programs.

Suspect in UWS gold bar scam sought
NEW YORK (1010 WINS) — The NYPD released surveillance footage Thursday asking for the public's help to identify a man wanted in connection with a $9 million grand larceny scam on the Upper West Side.
According to officials, a 67-year-old man was targeted after receiving a fake computer security alert claiming his financial assets were compromised. The victim was manipulated into making multiple transactions totaling $9 million to purchase several gold bars meant to "secure" his funds. On April 16, 2025, the victim met the unidentified suspect near West 81st Street and Broadway, handed over the gold bars, and the suspect fled on foot. No physical injuries were reported, and police are continuing their search for the suspect.
