articles.title_orig: Andy Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than we gained’ through Brexit
articles.title_zh: Andy Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than we gained’ through Brexit
articles.content_orig:
PM accuses Tories of burning ‘all our bridges’ and says deal he is pursuing with EU will ‘get food prices down’
Andy Burnham has said the UK has “lost more than we gained” since leaving the EU, the prime minister’s latest in a string of comments criticising Brexit.
Outlining his desire to form closer ties with Brussels, Burnham accused the Conservative party of having “burned all our bridges” with the bloc after Brexit and said a new deal he hopes to secure with the EU next week will “get food prices down” and put more money in the pockets of British exporters.
The prime minister is due to meet European leaders at a summit next week and secure agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4% – about £17bn – including on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. He will also “explore options” for a different long-term relationship with Brussels.
Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday, Burnham said: “We need to be willing to take difficult decisions to get the cost of living down.
“It’s why, in a few days’ time, I will head to the next UK-EU summit and I will be working hard as we move towards it to get to a new deal on food and farming between the UK and the EU. Why am I doing that? Because I want to help Welsh businesses.
The prime minister added: “I think we’ve lost more than we’ve gained over the last 10 years, and, actually, I think the Conservatives gave Britain a harsher and harder Brexit than people thought they were getting when they voted in 2016, because they burned all of our bridges in the aftermath, with the EU, and so I’m going to lead as prime minister on this issue, and I’m going to go and try and get the best deal I can for Wales, for those here who could benefit, Welsh farmers, exporters of Welsh shellfish and Welsh lamb.”
Burnham has recently said he is open to rejoining the single market, customs union or to “go all the way” by rejoining the EU, but on Saturday he said voters would ultimately be “the boss” of any changes.
He reiterated his commitment to Labour’s manifesto “red lines” – which rule out returning to the customs union, single market or free movement. “People working together in unions, trade unions, but also unions of nations, and that’s what makes us who we are,” he told the conference.
“And, yes, working with the European Union , as I said, but at the same time respecting the red lines in our manifesto and respecting the referendum, the referendum result. So, that’s the spirit, everybody, that I will take forward.”
The government has already made several announcements that would tie the UK closer to Brussels. Earlier this month, the Guardian reported that the UK was prepared to spend up to £450m a year to give EU students discounted university tuition fees, if Brussels allowed Britain access to the Made in Europe industrial programme.
Earlier this week, Hamish Falconer, the cabinet minister in charge of EU talks, said Britain was willing to discuss paying towards infrastructure schemes in poorer parts of the EU in return for access to the European electricity market.
after newsletter promotion
Despite Burnham’s recent pro-EU comments, senior figures in Brussels have said they want to see the UK begin to start paying for access to the European schemes it says it wants access to.
The EU’s former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier told the BBC last week: “There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market.”
Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, and António Costa, who leads the European Council, will meet Burnham on 20 November in Brussels for a summit where deals on food and drink, carbon emissions and youth exchange could be signed.
Barnier said the UK could not rejoin the single market “à la carte”, when speaking to the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg last Sunday, adding: “I said very, very often during these negotiations, the Brexit, there is no cherrypicking.”

articles.title_orig: Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres
articles.title_zh: Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of people have joined a protest in Edinburgh against the building of large-scale AI data centres.
Demonstrators with placards - and some dressed in costume - assembled at the top of the Royal Mile before marching towards the Scottish Parliament.
The event comes at a time of widespread debate about the environmental impact of data centres and is part of a wave of protests across Europe.
The Scottish government will soon publish new planning guidance on data centres and said it was developing a strategy to maximise the "public benefit".
Innovation Minister Alyn Smith recently said data centres were "the whisky bonds of the AI sector".
However protesters made it clear they disagree - carrying slogans such as "AI data centres threaten humanity" and "AI data centres: costing the Earth".
Some attended to voice their opposition to plans for data centres in particular communities - including Cockenzie, East Lothian, and Larbert, Falkirk.
Kim Cairns, a campaigner for 'Say No To Chapelcross AI Data Centre', told BBC Scotland News her community was worried about noise, road closures and access problems during the construction phase.
She was also concerned about the noise the centre would generate when it was operational.
Kim said: "It's not going to enrich anybody's lives. For Chapelcross it's the sheer size of it, the amount of electricity it's going to need.
"At the moment it's green fields with sheep and cows in it. It's going to be a monstrosity on the environment.
"The air pollution, the light pollution - it's just not needed."
AI is seen by some as the most transformative technology ever made but others have warned there is chance that if the frightening pace of development continues it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.
Meanwhile, Scotland's data centre debate centres around the scale and impact of the sites themselves.
At the moment, the biggest data centre in Scotland is thought to be DataVita's site in Airdrie, North Lanarkshire, which has a capacity for 12MW.
But if one planned for Chapelcross, Dumfries and Galloway, goes ahead it will have a capacity of 1,000MW - making it one of the largest data centres in the world.
The Scottish Greens and campaign groups have called for a moratorium on large data centres, arguing they could undermine climate targets and place additional pressure on renewable energy supplies.
The innovation minister previously told BBC Scotland some of the discourse around the subject was "wild".
Smith said: "You'd think there wasn't a planning system at all.
"Comparing a really bad data centre in the middle of the Utah desert doesn't track through to what we're going to have in Scotland."
Friends of the Earth campaigner Kim Pratt believes the people of Scotland should have the final say on the building of data centres.
She said: "The way that these data centres are being proposed is going to make a lot of profit for big tech companies but they're going to have huge impacts for people in Scotland.
"These developments are so massive they're going to have national-level impacts -they're energy hungry developments.
"There would be a massive increase in our energy bills but also in terms of climate impact as well.
"The Scottish government is only taking a few months to consider these impacts - and these developments are so new, we don't know what all the impacts will be."
The Scottish government confirmed it would publish new planning guidance on data centres before the end of the year and was "developing a strategic approach to maximising the public benefit from data centres located in Scotland".
A spokesperson added: "Planning authorities are also now required to notify ministers of new data centre applications, with a new planning direction also mandating an Environmental Impact Assessment to be submitted during planning for all new data centres with a power capacity exceeding 50 megawatts."

SpaceX succesfully launched its Starship Flight 15 mission on Friday, Nov. 13 , at 5:47 p.m. EDT (2247 GMT) from Starbase, Texas. Starship Flight 15 will attempt to land its Ship upper stage for the first time, but did abort a landing pad catch of its Super Heavy Booster. It will be the first-ever recovery of an orbital Starship upper stage, if successful. See launch video above and live views from SpaceX .

Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.
Ship has officially reentered Earth's atmosphere on its planned trip back to Texas' Starbase site for a historic "chopsticks" catch. The effects of our air on the vehicle are obvious; super-hot plasma now surrounds Ship's leading edges as it continues its descent.
All remains on schedule for a catch attempt around 4:16 p.m. EST (2116 GMT).
SpaceX just gave us some more information about why the Super Heavy booster aborted its chopsticks-catch try shortly after Starship's Flight 15 launch yesterday (Nov. 13).
"Early indications are that the booster ended its boostback [burn] early due to a low fuel mass alarm," SpaceX's Kate Tice said today (Nov. 14) during the company's Flight 15 webcast (which is ongoing, as Starship's Ship upper stage is currently coming back to Earth for its own catch , a milestone scheduled to occur at around 4:16 p.m. EST, 2116 GMT).
"The team is still investigating the root cause on that," Tice added. "However, booster guidance then detected that it wasn't in the right position as it was flying back, so the booster correctly aborted itself from the tower catch and went for an offshore water divert instead."
Starship 's Ship upper stage just began its descent back toward Earth. At about 3:23 p.m. EST (1823 GMT) today (Nov. 14), the vehicle conducted a 10-second, single-engine deorbit burn that went according to plan.
"Good deorbit burn," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during SpaceX's webcast today. "Starship [is] on its way back through the atmosphere soon."
Ship remains on target to return to SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas for a catch by the launch tower's "chopstick" arms at around 4:16 p.m. EST (2116 GMT) — about 22.5 hours after it launched from the same pad on Starship's 15th test flight.
Good news, space fans: A "chopsticks" catch attempt of Starship 's Ship upper stage is officially on for this afternoon (Nov. 14).
"Moments ago, the launch team conducted the final planned contingency check for Ship's return to the launch site," SpaceX' s Kate Tice said during a webcast update today. "And, great news: All teams have polled 'go.' That included Stage 2, heat shield, flaps, structures, aero, guidance, navigation and control and, of course, the tower."
If all goes to plan, Ship will return to SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, where it will be snagged by its launch tower's arms at around 4:16 p.m. EST (2116 GMT), bringing an end to Starship Flight 15 , which launched on Friday evening (Nov. 13). SpaceX has never tried a chopsticks catch with Ship before, so tune in here at Space.com to see how it goes!
We just got some updated information about Super Heavy's landing abort during Starship Flight 15. SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot initially said that the booster diverted away from a "chopsticks" catch attempt at Starbase on Friday (Nov. 13) due to a guidance, navigation and control (GNC) issue. This morning (Nov. 14), however, he exonerated the GNC system, saying it performed as expected during Super Heavy's return to Earth.
The GNC system "detected that the booster was not in the place that it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch, did an automated abort and then headed out to that offshore splashdown location," Huot said. "The team's still digging into the root cause on how we got there, and so, more to come on that."
You can read our story about Super Heavy's landing abort here .
SpaceX is still planning to catch Starship's Ship upper stage at Starbase today. Everything looks good for that unprecedented attempt, which will occur at around 4:16 p.m. EST (2116 GMT), if all goes according to plan. You can watch it live here at Space.com.
We are now 16 hours into SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission , with just over six more hours remaining until the Ship 42 upper stage makes its attempted landing catch back at Starbase.
In an earlier post, I discussed SpaceX's update on how a guidance system issue caused the Super Heavy booster landing abort just after liftoff. You can now read my full story on the Super Heavy landing abort here .
Space.com's Josh Dinner captured the moment the Super Heavy booster triggered its flight termination system to explode in the Gulf of Mexico offshore from Starbase. Check it out.
Until the landing abort, the Starship Super Heavy booster performed as expected during its liftoff and stage separation, delivering its Ship upper stage to the proper position to fire its own engines and reach orbit.
Here's a stunning look at all 33 Super Heavy Raptor engines firing in unison to power the 41-story rocket's ascent into orbit, as seen by Josh.
The next Flight 15 milestone for SpaceX will be a "Final Hawaii Return Check" at the 20-hours, 41-minute mark of the mission. That will be a go/no-go moment when SpaceX decides whether to attempt the Starbase chopsticks landing at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT) for Ship 42, or direct it to a splashdown off the coast of Hawaii.
Our landing livestream will begin at about that check in time, at 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT).
Good morning and happy Saturday, Space Fans! Today is Flight Day 2 for SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 test flight and SpaceX reports that its Ship 42 spacecraft is in good health as we near the 14-hour mark of its 22.5-hour test flight.
About 7 hours into the mission, SpaceX spokesman Dan Huot confirmed that flight controllers gave the go-ahead to forgo an early return window for a splashdown off the coast of Chile and proceed for the full 14-orbit flight. Starship is on track for a landing attempt, its first-ever from orbit, today (Nov. 14) at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT) . Space.com's livestream of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 landing will begin at 2 p.m. EST and you can see it at the top of this page.
"Starship's going to stay in space. We are one step closer to an eventual return to launch site," Huot said in the update. "So that's great news."
Huot also reported that Starship's tile-covered heat shield appears in good shape for today's landing attempt. SpaceX used long-range ground-based cameras and cameras on some of the 26 Starlink satellites the Ship deployed to check its heat shield after liftoff.
"Our heat shield team reviewed all the data we got from our ground tracking cameras, and from those satellite cameras and confirmed the heat shield is in a good posture for a reentry and return to the launch site," Huot said.

articles.title_orig: How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips
articles.title_zh: How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO J ensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday.
Officials also said that Elon Musk , the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.
The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.
"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified.
"In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there."
Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, "The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement."
"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said.
Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue."
China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless.
Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed , a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.
The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.
During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.
"I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said.
"Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."

articles.title_orig: ‘GTA 6’ Reveals Jason And Lucia’s Limited Crime Options To Start
articles.title_zh: ‘GTA 6’ Reveals Jason And Lucia’s Limited Crime Options To Start
articles.content_orig:
Rockstar Games recently sat down to give their one-millionth interview about Grand Theft Auto 6. Not really, but it feels like that sometimes. In the interview, they discussed the open-world potential of GTA 6, which releases worldwide next week. They spoke about crime and punishment, how the characters develop alongside one another, and how you can have ’empathy’ this time around.
While talking and playing the game during the interview, Rockstar’s Rob Nelson, who is fast becoming the PR face of GTA 6, explained how the story progresses with Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, the game’s co-protagonists. Like other games in the series, and in games like Red Dead, you start as a relatively small fish in a big pond.
Grand Theft Auto 6 represents the pinnacle of freedom; that much is certain. From what we’ve seen in the trailers released thus far, we’re getting a gargantuan world absolutely brimming with opportunities to explore, enjoy what’s on offer, and yes, wreak a little havoc.
But it’s not all about being a nasty criminal this time around. Rockstar recently confirmed that you can have empathy in this game for the first time in franchise history.
Rob Nelson spoke to The Guardian about the concept of crime in GTA 6, and he laid out the inner workings of the game’s story. As Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, the loved-up dual protagonists of this game, you’re not immediately able to waltz into a high-end jewelry store and make your fortune.
It’s a staggered, tiered system, it sounds like.
The interview context explains how the pair ‘can’t just steal any car or bust their way into a bank’ right out of the gate. Players will start by hotwiring low-end vehicles and picking ‘basic locks’, robbing convenience stores and gas stations before working their way up to the bigger, heftier targets.
We’ve already heard how certain cars will provide blockers to being stolen, boasting intelligent anti-theft systems, alarms, trackers, and immobilizers. We know how some store clerks will fight back, how passers-by will identify you to the police, and how people will record things on their phones, giving you a digital footprint.
It’s a fairly natural thing to assume that we wouldn’t start GTA 6 as master criminals, but in the trailers that we’ve seen thus far, we know we’re working towards that . We’ve seen Jason and Lucia robbing some pretty intense locations, decked out in body armor and wielding sophisticated weapons.
We’ve also seen them wearing Hawaiian shirts and carrying a basic handgun to empty the register in a liquor store, so the spectrum is well and truly there.
Rob Nelson explained in the interview:
These guys are a younger couple with their backs against the wall. Narratively, it doesn’t make a lot of sense for them to go out and cause as much carnage and make as much noise as they can.
Thanks to GameRoll on socials for the heads up.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is just a few days away from hitting the market. Are you looking forward to the game? Let us know your thoughts on the Insider Gaming Discord server .

articles.title_orig: Driver Stops in Front of Moving Car, Then Gets Mad When Motorist Goes Around: "Road Rage Or Insurance Scam?"
articles.title_zh: Driver Stops in Front of Moving Car, Then Gets Mad When Motorist Goes Around: "Road Rage Or Insurance Scam?"
articles.content_orig:
A driver traveling on a rain-soaked road had to stop suddenly when another motorist moved into their lane and slammed on the brakes. The close call was only the start of an encounter that soon drew thousands of reactions online.
Dashcam footage shared on Reddit on November 8 shows the confrontation on a suburban road. According to the person who posted the video, the other driver came to a complete stop, leaving little room to get around.
The motorist said the other driver began yelling and making rude gestures before following their vehicle. What started as a possible rear-end crash had turned into a confrontation that continued even after the cars separated.
Now, people watching the clip are arguing over what caused the strange behavior. Some suspect road rage, while others think the driver may have been trying to cause a crash for an insurance claim.
The original Reddit post , shared by u/pooh_jo in r/dashcams, describes a drive that took an unexpected turn.
The recording begins on a wet suburban road, with other vehicles traveling nearby. As the dashcam vehicle moves forward, another car enters its lane and slows sharply before coming to a stop.
The driver behind manages to avoid hitting it, but getting past is another problem. According to the person who posted the footage, they had to reverse before there was enough space to drive around the stopped vehicle.
Rather than simply continuing down the road, the other motorist reportedly became angry. The person behind the dashcam described the driver yelling, making an obscene gesture, and later flashing their headlights while following.
The person who posted the video could not explain why the other motorist behaved that way. In the original description, they wrote, "I have no idea if this was some sort of road rage or insurance scam."
That question quickly took over the comments. One Reddit user wrote, "Honestly seems like an Insurance scam." Others agreed, pointing to the wet pavement and sudden stop as reasons for concern.
Not everyone accepted that explanation. Some commenters thought the driver might have been upset about the dashcam vehicle's speed and was trying to force it to slow down.
Another viewer suggested that a person planning an insurance scam would likely have driven away once the attempted collision failed. The continued confrontation, in that user's view, looked more like someone trying to make a point.
Neither explanation has been established. The post contains no evidence of an insurance claim or a confirmed motive for the other driver's actions.
The discussion also turned toward the person recording the footage. Several commenters questioned whether the dashcam driver was traveling too quickly for the rainy conditions.
Others pushed back, arguing that the vehicle appeared to leave enough room for nearby traffic and that the driver responded carefully to the sudden stop. One commenter claimed the posted speed was only slightly above the road's limit, though that limit has not been independently confirmed.
The argument soon shifted from the dashcam vehicle's speed to whether either driver had the right to confront another motorist over their driving.
One commenter put it simply: "Explanation doesn't equal excuse."
The person who shared the footage did not report a collision in their description. Instead, they described escaping the stopped vehicle only to have the other driver flash their lights and follow afterward.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang had a strict meetings rule for his 60 reports—Nvidia’s interim CEO has a similar mantra
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang had a strict meetings rule for his 60 reports—Nvidia’s interim CEO has a similar mantra
articles.content_orig:
President Trump suggested on Thursday that Tim Cook, former CEO of Apple, should become the leader of chip maker Nvidia following its chief executive Jensen Huang ’s resignation over his alleged affairs with two women.
“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend! ” Trump posted on TruthSocial.
Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday morning, in the wake of reports that he had allegedly been involved in two affairs, including one with a woman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese spy.
It is unclear if Trump has reached out to Cook regarding this suggestion. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Huang and the White House have maintained a close relationship since the start of Trump’s second term. During his official visit to China in May, Trump invited Huang to attend the summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The New York Times reported that the President insisted on inviting Huang to join the delegation despite concerns over Huang’s relationship with a woman who is believed to be a Chinese spy.
Speaking with reporters on Monday, Trump repeatedly downplayed Huang’s alleged affair, insisting that he believed the tech billionaire’s assertion that he knew nothing about the alleged espionage operation.
“I really believe him,” Trump told reporters during the White House press conference. “I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

Tesla is doubling, or perhaps tripling down on its bold claims of an autonomous future with the offer to “select customers” to purchase a Cybercab for “personal use.” But the gilded, steering-wheel-free two-seater will “only be available in supported service areas” — meaning you’ll only be able to buy one if you live in one of the cities where Tesla currently operates its Robotaxi service.
The price of a Cybercab is listed at $29,990, plus a mandatory $299-a-month “Autonomy Subscription.” Tesla’s Robotaxi account on X announced the new offer, including screenshots of the order page and the invite email. But don’t expect a fleet of personally owned Cybercabs to suddenly materialize on public roads: “Initial availability is limited,” the invitation email warns.
Tesla began offering rides in the Cybercab as part of its Model Y-powered Robotaxi service in Austin in September. The company now has 278 Cybercabs in operation, representing approximately 40 percent of its fleet, according to the crowd-sourced Robotaxi Tracker.
The inclusion of a mandatory $299/month subscription is sure to rankle some fans who may have dreamed of cruising around in a $30,000 driverless Tesla, as originally promised by Tesla CEO Elon Musk when he first introduced the Cybercab in 2024. Musk made no mention of the Autonomy Subscription at that event, though it shouldn’t come as too much of a surprise given the $99/month fee Tesla currently charges for its Full Self-Driving (FSD) feature.
Still, that money adds up over time. Over a standard 5-year ownership period, the mandatory $299/month fee adds $17,940 to the sticker price (even with the first month included), bringing the real baseline cost to roughly $47,600 before taxes, charging, and insurance — more than a brand-new Model 3 or Model Y that you can actually drive anywhere in the country.
Unlike a standard Tesla where canceling FSD just reverts the car to manual driving, canceling the $299/month Autonomy Subscription renders the Cybercab completely unusable on public roads because there is no manual fallback. In effect, the car becomes a brick. Additionally, Tesla says that buyers will have to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit just to get in line for a December delivery window that isn’t guaranteed.
One of the biggest selling points of Musk’s 2024 “We, Robot” pitch was that regular people could buy a Cybercab and add it to Tesla’s Robotaxi network to earn passive income while they sleep or work. But the order terms explicitly prohibit owners from using the vehicle for commercial purposes — meaning no Uber, no DoorDash, and no putting it on Tesla’s own Robotaxi network to offset the $299/month fee. Tesla AI chief Ashok Elluswamy has floated Q2 2027 as a possible target for letting customer cars join the network, so early buyers are paying full freight with zero way to monetize the car.
Moreover, Tesla only has to give you 30 days’ warning before raising the price. If they update the rules and you keep using the service, you automatically agree to the new terms. Also, if you cancel — or if Tesla suspends your access — you won’t get a partial refund for the rest of the month you already paid for.
Of course, that’s just the fine print. On X, Tesla CEO Elon Musk was promising a much wider rollout, subject — of course — to “regulatory approval.” Musk frequently frames regulatory approval as the primary external bottleneck holding back his robotaxi timelines as a way to shift focus away from Tesla’s technological shortcomings.
(For what it’s worth, he also called his own company’s $299/month Autonomy Subscription “too high,” arguing that it should actually be $115/month or closer to Tesla’s $99/month Full Self-Driving subscription.)
But Musk seemed more focused on taunting YouTuber Marques Brownlee , who promised to shave his head if Tesla delivered a Cybercab for under $30,000 before 2027, than answering any of the litany of safety and liability questions raised by this offer. (For his part, Brownlee says he thinks his hair is safe.)
For starters, how does Tesla plan on selling a vehicle that doesn’t comply with current Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards that require traditional controls like steering wheels and pedals? Tesla says the Autonomy Subscription covers autonomous driving, maintenance, and towing, but explicitly excludes auto insurance. The company hasn’t explained how personal auto insurers will underwrite a car with no human driver, or how liability is split between the owner and Tesla if the vehicle causes an accident while operating autonomously. Nor has Tesla disclosed how it selects invited buyers or how many units are earmarked for private sale versus its internal fleet.
Then there is the small matter of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration already opening a formal audit into how Tesla self-certified a vehicle without a steering wheel, pedals, or side mirrors. Tesla submitted its legal justification to NHTSA in October, requested that the entire response be kept confidential, and is now taking customer deposits while NHTSA’s ruling is still pending.
Which means early buyers aren’t just paying $47,600 for a geofenced car they aren’t allowed to drive — they’re putting down non-refundable cash on a vehicle the federal government hasn’t even decided is street-legal.

articles.title_orig: Kim Jong Un Remakes North Korea’s Flag, Ditching Soviet-Era Version
articles.title_zh: Kim Jong Un Remakes North Korea’s Flag, Ditching Soviet-Era Version
articles.content_orig:
SEOUL, Nov. 13 (Yonhap) -- North Korea has revised its constitution to change its national flag's aspect ratio for the first time since its regime was established in 1948, according to the amended basic law posted on the website of Pyongyang's propaganda outlet.
Article 166 of the revised constitution posted on Naenara's website stipulates that the ratio of the flag's height to its width is 1 to 1.65, replacing the previous ratio of 1 to 2.
The change came as North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has sought to build his own governing style and national identity while retaining some legacies of his predecessors.
The flag's 1-to-2 ratio rule had remained unchanged in the law until the North's constitutional revision in September 2023.
Despite the ratio change, the overall design of the North's flag remains intact, consisting of a broad red stripe in the center, narrow white stripes above and below it, blue stripes above and below the white stripes, and a red five-pointed star in a white circle.
The constitution says the red stripe stands for the blood shed by anti-Japan fighters who dedicated their lives to defending the country's freedom and independence during Japan's 1910-45 colonial rule. The white circle and two white stripes symbolize people's loyalty to the nation's leader and ruling Workers' Party of Korea.
The two blue stripes represent the revolutionary spirit of the people struggling for peace, friendship and unity in the world, as well as the country's sovereignty, it said.
Observers said the change in the flag's aspect ratio might have reflected Pyongyang's efforts to craft a new national image under the incumbent leader Kim, the third-generation hereditary ruler.

articles.title_orig: Lord Mayor’s Show takes place through City of London streets
articles.title_zh: Lord Mayor’s Show takes place through City of London streets
articles.content_orig:
By JAKE HOLDEN, UK NEWS REPORTER
Published: 10:34 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 10:36 EST, 14 November 2026
London streets have been filled with punters trying to catch a glimpse of the pomp and ceremony of the Lord Mayor's Show.
The ancient 800-year-old tradition sees a huge procession of marching bands take over the Square Mile, along with iconic cockney Pearly Queens and Kings and other light-hearted traditional British pageantry.
This year there is even a robot to welcome in the modern age.
It will be led by the brand-new Lord Mayor, Alderman Bronek Masojada, 64, of the Billingsgate ward.
He will be the 698th Lord Mayor of the City of London, succeeding Lady Mayor Dame Susan Langley DBE - the first to take the title Lady Mayor, though not the first female Lord Mayor.
A new one is elected every year on September 29. They are then sworn in the day before the Lord Mayor's Show to lead the festivities.
The office of Lord Mayor is not to be confused with the Mayor of London, currently Sadiq Khan. The former is largely a ceremonial ambassadorial office which began in 1189, and its jurisdiction is kept within the confines of the City of London.
Lord Mayor Masojada - a global leader in the insurance industry - said: 'It is a profound honour to be elected as Lord Mayor of the City of London.
'I will showcase the many British opportunities, persuade British and international capital to invest in those opportunities, and champion talent, both local and global.'
The 698th Lord Mayor of the City of London Alderman Bronek Masojada, 64, waves to crowds from the State Coach
Iconic cockney East End Pearly Queens and Kings join the procession in the Square Mile
A robot was seen joining the march, welcoming the modern age to this ancient 800-year-old tradition
The Lord Mayor inspects servicemen during the festivities ahead of the march
Members of the Polish community take part in the Lord Mayor's Show. The Lord Mayor is of Polish descent but was born in South Africa
A marching band plays in their bear-skin hats while following the parade
There are all sorts of whimsical pageantry involved in the parade these days as it has evolved over centuries
The three-mile parade through the heart of the Square Mile features over 6,500 participants, 250 horses, and more than 50 decorated floats
The show is one of the world's oldest and longest civic procession
Servicemen and women take part, backed by old military vehicles in London's streets
Liverymen carry oars and escort the coach. The oars are an homage to the Mayor's barge, which used to be rowed down the Thames by members of the Company of Watermen and Lightermen
While older military vehicles made an appearance, so too did their more modern counterparts
Vintage steam-powered cars made their way through the streets behind
Finely dressed marching bands all added to the busy atmosphere
They started the parade at Mansion House and walked down past St Paul's Cathedral, then all the way down Fleet Street to the Royal Courts of Justice
The return route began at Temple on the Embankment and went back up to Mansion House
An inflatable balloon shaped as a piece of meat was towed along by butchers in the parade
Bagpipers play as they stride past the west entrance of St Paul's Cathedral
Children got involved in the marching bands and donned the red ceremonial uniforms
There were 250 horses included in the parade this year
The vibrant annual show dates back to 1215, when King John decreed that each new holder of the position should go to Westminster to swear an oath of loyalty.
King John created the office himself in a hopeless attempt to try to appease the barons as they grew more impatient with his poor leadership.
Since then, the ceremony has changed and grown a great deal.
Lord Mayor Alderman Bronek Masojada waved to crowds from the window of the exquisitely gilded State Coach, as is tradition.
He wore the Lord Mayor's ceremonial red robes and black feathered hat for the event and inspected the servicemen on show ahead of the parade.
Once this was done, he hopped into the golden State Coach - first used in 1757 for the procession to travel from Mansion House, the Lord Mayor's official residence, to the Royal Courts of Justice in the Strand.
Once at the Courts, Lord Mayor Masojada was photographed swearing an oath of allegiance to the sovereign - as was done all those years ago when King John began the tradition.
Lord Mayor Masojada is of Polish descent but was born in South Africa, where he was raised and educated, studying Civil Engineering at the University of KwaZulu-Natal.
Lord Mayor of the City of London Alderman Bronek Masojada was sworn in as the 698th person to hold the position at Guildhall. His predecessor, Lady Mayoress, Dame Susan Langley, sits on the right
Lord Mayor Masojada and his wife Jane pose for photos after the Silent Ceremony at Guildhall
He also completed national service as a lieutenant in the South African Army.
He then moved into the world of insurance and became the Chief Executive of Hiscox in London in 2000, stepping down in 2021.
He was elected as alderman for the ward of Billingsgate in 2019 and served as one of the two Sheriffs of London for 2023/24 - a mandatory prerequisite for being made mayor.

articles.title_orig: Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%
articles.title_zh: Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%
articles.content_orig:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.
Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.
The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.
The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.
Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August .
Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.
After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.
They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.
Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.
We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q , released last Saturday , indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.
It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.
As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.
On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.
Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.
If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.
The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."
The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.
Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders .
In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.
Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each , and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.
That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.
The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.
Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.
In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.
All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.
In a term sheet filed early Friday , Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.
Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.
It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.
In April , Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.
Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.
Some links may require a subscription:
Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, " The Intelligent Investor ," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.
WARREN BUFFETT : On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, " Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits " and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.
You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] " The Intelligent Investor ," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.
Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...
One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.
And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.
And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang’s spy scandal isn’t a one-off
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang’s spy scandal isn’t a one-off
articles.content_orig:
Chinese intelligence is working the AI industry’s top floors. Tech companies aren’t prepared — and the FBI agents who should be watching have been sent elsewhere.
Chinese intelligence is working the AI industry’s top floors. Tech companies aren’t prepared — and the FBI agents who should be watching have been sent elsewhere.
Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia after reports of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy is being treated as a one-off scandal. But it’s not. In the past year, my private security firm, which is staffed largely by former intelligence and law enforcement officers, has handled a number of cases in which senior executives at U.S. technology companies had relationships with women who we came to believe were working for Chinese intelligence.
The artificial intelligence industry has a security problem that it does not yet fully understand. U.S. companies are building technology with massive commercial and national security value, but their defenses against foreign intelligence are, in most cases, nowhere near good enough. At the same time, the FBI counterintelligence squads that should help protect these companies are badly understaffed; some agents have been reassigned to focus on the administration’s (opens in new tab) political priorities, while others have been purged (opens in new tab) . The result is a widening gap between how much the technology matters and how well it’s being protected.
The FBI’s counterintelligence posture is an important part of this picture. NPR (opens in new tab) reported in October (opens in new tab) that in many of the bureau’s 56 field offices, counterintelligence squads are only 50%-60% staffed, as agents and analysts have been shifted toward fighting violent crime and enforcing immigration laws. The FBI disputes that this has weakened its counterintelligence operation. But it’s hard to believe these kinds of cuts haven’t affected China-focused efforts — and they come at a time when U.S. AI and AI-adjacent firms are more at risk from foreign interference than ever.
Investigating crime is important, but moving experienced personnel away from counterintelligence is a dangerous trade. Counterintelligence investigations are exceedingly complex and depend on accumulated knowledge and specialized judgment built over decades. That expertise is easy to lose and slow to rebuild. The history of intelligence shows that political purges take years to recover from.
After 9/11, for example, the FBI redirected large numbers of agents away from white-collar crime to counterterrorism. By the time the 2008 financial crisis hit, the bureau had fewer people to investigate mortgage and securities fraud — one reason so few of the people responsible ever faced charges.
In this new environment, technology companies can’t assume that government agencies will spot a suspicious relationship or intervene before valuable information leaves the organization. They need their own insider-risk programs to recognize foreign interference and respond. But in my experience, much of the industry treats protection against espionage as an extension of conventional cybersecurity or physical security, rather than what it is: a distinct investigative discipline that must operate across the whole business, from the engineers writing code to the data centers and supply chains — and, as the Huang case shows, must reach all the way to the top.
OpenAI had some success this year when its internal teams found bugging equipment (opens in new tab) planted by a Saudi national; however, in most cases, the affected company either has no security team or has the wrong kind, and the warnings come from a worried colleague. That’s lucky, but not a sustainable defense.
One reason companies miss these operations is that foreign interference rarely feels urgent. A death threat creates an obvious reason to act. A relationship that gradually opens access to sensitive information can look ambiguous or commercially useful or be too uncomfortable to question. Executives may hesitate because they fear disrupting a commercial partnership or creating an internal controversy. To be blunt: Spies don’t often look like spies.
This is why board and executive attention matters. Security teams cannot manage risk if leadership treats it as peripheral. Companies need clear responsibility for assessing suspicious approaches, preserving relevant evidence, and deciding when an issue warrants investigation. They also need to accept that a credible inquiry may produce inconvenient findings. A security team that lacks authority to examine sensitive relationships will struggle, regardless of its budget.
The practical starting point for a company that suspects it may be the target of foreign interference is to commission an independent review through outside counsel, supported by experienced investigators. Done properly, with the work genuinely structured around legal advice, that arrangement can keep the findings privileged, which matters when the subject of the inquiry may be the company’s own leadership. The value lies in combining investigative competence with disciplined legal oversight.
Companies should also not assume that operations in the United Kingdom or European Union are inherently insulated from these risks. For a U.S. company, an overseas subsidiary or partner may become an indirect route to sensitive information. Security assessments therefore need to follow actual access across borders and corporate structures.
Ultimately, the AI boom has made American tech companies some of the world’s most valuable intelligence targets. Their defenses have failed to keep pace, and the government agencies that might have caught what the companies miss are looking elsewhere. Much has been made of the U.S. retreat from Europe’s defenses. Less noticed is the U.S. retreat from protecting its own technology companies.
Roderick Jones is executive chairman of Concentric, a San Francisco-based security firm. He began his career in Scotland Yard’s Special Branch.

articles.title_orig: Qatar and Turkey announce a landmark defence alliance
articles.title_zh: Qatar and Turkey announce a landmark defence alliance
articles.content_orig:
Here's a rundown of all the news you need to know for Saturday, including Türkiye and Qatar signing five agreements, including a mutual defense pact, during the 12th meeting of the Türkiye-Qatar High Strategic Committee in Istanbul; the US Federal Aviation Administration lifting a nationwide flight ground stop after a telecommunications outage; and US President Donald Trump set to hold trilateral talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen next week, according to the White House.
Türkiye and Qatar signed five agreements, including a mutual defense pact, during the 12th meeting of the Türkiye-Qatar High Strategic Committee in Istanbul, with the signing ceremony held at the Presidential Dolmabahce Office in the presence of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.
Erdogan and Sheikh Tamim signed the mutual defense agreement, while the other deals cover consumer protection, education, and cooperation on peace, reconciliation and conflict resolution.
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani signed the memorandum on peace, reconciliation and conflict resolution, along with a joint declaration marking the committee’s 12th meeting.
The US Federal Aviation Administration lifted a nationwide ground stop at airports after a telecommunications outage affecting Air Route Traffic Control Centers prompted authorities to halt flights as a precaution, with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy describing the problem as a "communication issue" and "an emergency."
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that the public was "never" in danger and that there was "no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack."
"We’re not ruling out anything," Mullin said when asked about a possible cyberattack, while the FAA said every flight had been accounted for and international flights would be handled case by case.
Separately, Microsoft said it had "no indication" the ground stop was related to any of its services, while FlightAware said more than 10,000 flights were delayed or canceled.
US President Donald Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen next week on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, with assistant White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales saying he will discuss reducing nuclear weapons, whose proliferation Trump believes is "very dangerous."
A senior US official said Washington does not expect an agreement, calling the talks "the entry point, the first conversation" at the leader level, and said Trump plans to raise Iran but not Ukraine because China is not part of the separate US-Russia track.
Trump will leave Washington on Monday for Manila for a Quad leaders’ meeting and the US-ASEAN Special Summit, then travel to Shenzhen on Wednesday, where he will hold a meeting and working lunch with Xi on Thursday before the trilateral meeting. Another senior US official described the Trump-Xi session as an "implementation check-in” on the trade agreement, with no tariff changes expected.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk will join Trump for parts of his visit to China but will not participate in official meetings, according to US officials.
- A 9-month-old Palestinian baby, Kinan Ahmed Arqiq, died of severe hypothermia in the Gaza Strip, the first recorded cold-related death of the winter, the Health Ministry said.
- Israel’s Arab Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen has hinted at informal talks with the Jewish opposition in the Knesset and outlined demands including repealing the Kaminitz Law on home demolitions and adopting a plan to tackle crime.
- Türkiye’s law ratifying the "Mecca Agreement for Joint Defense" with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia was published in the Official Gazette and took effect upon publication, after parliament approved it 279-119 on Nov. 5.
- International Criminal Court judges have ordered the formal closure of the court’s original Afghanistan investigation, which included allegations against US troops, saying the prosecution had not shown it could "effectively carry out any further investigative or prosecutorial activities," while a separate probe into alleged Taliban crimes since August 2021 continues.
- Polish President Karol Nawrocki has vetoed for a second time legislation implementing key provisions of the EU’s Digital Services Act, arguing it would give officials excessive control over online speech, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk criticized the move.
- Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones sought to reassure employees following Jensen Huang’s resignation, with Kress thanking staff for their "resilience, professionalism and continued dedication" in internal emails published by The Verge.
- A Syrian soldier was killed and two others were injured in an attack by unidentified gunmen in Jadid Bakara town in the eastern province of Deir ez-Zor, the Defense Ministry said.
- US visa restrictions have forced Zambia to withdraw its Miss Universe contestant and left Zimbabwe’s Roseanna Hall uncertain of competing in Puerto Rico less than two weeks before the final.
- A global Microsoft outage disrupted government and private services in the Asia-Pacific, with Japan’s government email services going down and New Zealand suspending all visa processing until further notice

articles.title_orig: Nearly €20m in cash found buried, hidden in Hungary corruption case
articles.title_zh: Nearly €20m in cash found buried, hidden in Hungary corruption case
articles.content_orig:
Anti-corruption agency carried out searches as part of investigation into Orbán-era minister accused of taking bribes
Hungary’s anti-corruption agency said on Friday it had seized cash worth $19.5m (£14.8m) buried in forests and hidden elsewhere while investigating an ex-minister of nationalist former leader Viktor Orbán’s cabinet.
Miklós Seszták, Hungary’s minister of national development between 2014 and 2018, is accused of taking bribes in a scheme involving the state transport company, purchasing secondhand buses at inflated prices.
The prime minister, Péter Magyar , won a landslide election victory in April, ending Orbán’s 16 years in power after promising to investigate alleged corruption and abuse of office during his rival’s rule.
Seszták, two other Orbán-era ministers and the former premier’s brother have been taken into custody in different cases as graft inquiries have gathered pace in recent weeks.
The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH), an anti-graft body with sweeping powers established as part of Magyar’s accountability drive, said it searched several locations on Thursday and Friday as part of the criminal proceedings against Seszták.
“During the search, investigators found large amounts of cash: buried in forests, hidden in agricultural and warehouse buildings as well as residential properties, and stored in high-value safes in secluded locations,” the statement said.
“The total amount of cash found during the two-day search was 5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and US $1,257,100,” it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m.
NVVH said its staff deposited the cash into the Hungarian State Treasury’s account.
“Upon receipt, 12 Treasury employees spent 8 hours counting the money using 5 counting machines,” the finance minister, András Kármán, said on Facebook.
Magyar hailed the seizure as a potential turning point.
“This officially marks the end of the Fidesz-KDNP mafia!” he said in reference to Orbán’s former governing coalition.
The former leader did not react to the latest development. Orbán had previously denounced the probes targeting his inner circle as “political persecution” aimed at imprisoning him.

Microsoft has confirmed that full service has been re-established following a widespread global IT disruption that affected schools, courts, businesses, police forces and the NHS.
The technology company announced on Saturday morning that functionality had returned for all remaining users affected by one of the most severe IT failures in recent years.
In a statement on its Microsoft 365 status page, the US-based firm stated: "We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions.
"Further updates can be found at MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center."
Addressing the cause on Friday, Microsoft stated that the disruption was due to a "technical issue not related to cyber or AI agents".
Users reported that Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Downdetector, an online tracker, said it received outage reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories.
The outage affected governments, courts, healthcare services, businesses, airlines and banks in many places. Governments including those of Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the hours-long episode had impacted some of their operations.
Emergency measures were activated by the UK government and international authorities, with Microsoft working to recover messaging, email and key services after they began failing around 6pm GMT on Thursday.
The National Pharmacy Association warned customers of delays in getting medication. The outage affected the National Health Service and threatened to prevent doctors from emailing prescriptions to pharmacies.
“Please bear with your pharmacy teams today, where waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions,” a spokesperson said.
Government cyber minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra noted that the failure mostly impacted back-office functions, with contingency plans put in place.
But she acknowledged there had been “limited reports of impact on frontline service delivery” and the incident had been “inconvenient and disruptive”.
The minister said she had spoken to Microsoft UK’s chief executive, Darren Hardman, about the situation.
Monitoring website Downdetector first showed a spike in users reporting problems with Microsoft Teams in the UK at about 6.15pm on Thursday, with more than 130,000 reporting Outlook issues in the US at its peak on Thursday night.
Millions of its customers were unable to send and receive emails through Outlook, with Teams, the tech giant’s Copilot AI assistant and other Microsoft 365 services also affected for many.
Other AI chat services were disrupted, such as OpenAI’s Chat GPT and Anthropic’s Claude.
Police forces in England and Wales said on Friday they were unable to receive crime reports online.
Meanwhile, NHS England said health service staff were “enacting long-standing measures” to overcome IT outages, including using paper records.

articles.title_orig: Russian casualties ‘reach 450,000’: What that means for the Ukraine war
articles.title_zh: Russian casualties ‘reach 450,000’: What that means for the Ukraine war
articles.content_orig:
Records leaked from Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, have shown that at least 450,000 Russians, most of them soldiers, died in the war in Ukraine up to August this year.
Among the dead were more than 4,000 foreign citizens who are believed to have died fighting for Russia, from countries including Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Nepal, Colombia and Nigeria.
The records were obtained by two hacking groups, the Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Ukraine’s Silent Crow.
Rosstat confirmed it had been hit by cyberattacks between October 29 and November 1, but said it found no evidence that its databases had been compromised or that protected data leaked.
Moscow does not officially publish its military death toll.
Deaths can take months, and sometimes years, to be registered, in Russia. Investigations for The Financial Times (FT) have concluded that once late paperwork is counted, the toll up to August will settle at about 550,000.
So what do the leaked records show, and what do they tell us about who is fighting Russia’s war? Here’s what you need to know:
The Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow said on November 1 that they had broken into Rosstat’s network.
The two hacking groups published their own analysis of the records and shared the files with several news organisations, though the data has not been independently verified.
However, media outlets and analysts say they believe it is real.
Janis Kluge, an expert on Russia at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, wrote on X: “There is no longer any doubt that the leaked Rosstat database is authentic. You can find any famous person who has died in recent years.”
However, in a later post he added: “The trickier question is: Was the data manipulated to increase the war death toll?” before adding, “This would [be] unbelievably difficult, so this is a highly unlikely conspiracy theory”.
A death toll far beyond anything Moscow has admitted so far.
The files list about 410,000 deaths directly as war-related, and 42,000 more fighting-age men whose deaths were confirmed in court because their bodies have never been recovered.
The FT identified another 12,000 likely military deaths among men who died at or near the front, bringing the total to at least 450,000.
About 120,000 of those with a recorded location died in the area containing Avdiivka and Pokrovsk, and a further 48,000 in Bakhmut, the FT reported.
Avdiivka is a small industrial city in the Donetsk region. After Russian-backed forces seized parts of eastern Ukraine in 2014 and 2015, it became part of the so-called “contact line”, and Ukrainian forces spent years fortifying the city.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it was the subject of two years of bitter fighting before Russia took it in 2024.
After the fall of Avdiivka, Russian forces moved towards the coal-mining city of Pokrovsk in the Donetsk region, capturing it in early 2026 after more than a year of gruelling battles that had left the city in ruins.
Bakhmut, a city in the Donetsk Oblast and situated at a vital intersection connecting eastern Ukraine with the rest of the country, was the site of the longest and bloodiest infantry battle of the war before falling to Russian and paramilitary Wagner Group forces in May 2023.
Older men from poorer, often minority regions.
The average age of those killed rose from 34 in the first year of the war to 40 in 2025, and men aged 35 to 44 made up the largest group, with 158,000 dead, the FT reported.
Ethnic Russians constitute more than two-thirds of Russia’s population of 143 million. The rest are minorities – from millions of ethnic Ukrainians and Tatars to smaller Indigenous groups in Siberia and the Arctic.
Zabaykalsky Krai, home to a large community of Buryats, an Indigenous Mongolic people of southern Siberia, recorded about 12,300 deaths, roughly one for every 80 people in the region, the FT reported.
Bashkortostan, another region with a large minority population including Indigenous Bashkirs and Volga Tatars, recorded 15,800 deaths.
More than 4,000, and possibly far more.
The FT identified 4,141 probable foreign soldiers holding foreign citizenship among the dead.
Bloomberg News, using a wider definition that includes people born outside Russia, counted 11,335, with foreign deaths rising from about 630 in 2022 to more than 5,500 in 2025.
Deaths of Nepalis were concentrated in 2023 and 2024, and those of Colombians, Kenyans and Nigerians from late 2025, Bloomberg reported.
The FT counted the highest death toll from Uzbekistan at 807, followed by Tajikistan with 598. There were also 44 Nepali dead and 98 Colombians, the highest toll from Latin America.
About 340 Africans are among the dead, most of them killed since 2025, Bloomberg reported.
Nigeria, Cameroon and Egypt had the highest tolls, with 127 deaths between them, according to the FT.
Furthermore, Ukrainian officials believe Russia deployed some 14,000 North Korean troops to hold off Ukraine’s 2024 incursion into the Kursk region, but they do not appear in the leaked data.
Mostly for the money, and often after being misled.
An estimated 28,000 foreigners from 136 countries are said to be fighting in the Russian army overall.
An Amnesty International report in September found that people from Brazil, Colombia, Sri Lanka and South Africa had been promised well-paid civilian jobs and then forced into the army on arrival in Russia.
The rights group spoke with foreign nationals currently serving with Russian forces and members of their families as well as lawyers, human rights activists and journalists.
It found local agents and misleading online job advertisements were being used to deceive foreign nationals in their home countries.
Nationals from 36 African countries are known to be fighting for Russia in the four-year war, Ukraine’s foreign minister said in November last year.
One South African man who applied online for a driving job in Poland was told to fly to Moscow, pick up a truck, and drive it to Poland.
His wife told Amnesty International: “Upon arrival to Moscow, everything was taken from him. He was told that he would not be going to Poland and that he is becoming a soldier.”
Many recruits were promised lucrative salaries and sign-up bonuses that were not then fulfilled, Amnesty reported.
In Kenya , where intelligence officials say more than 1,000 citizens have been recruited, agencies promised monthly wages of about $2,715 and bonuses of up to $9,309.
Moscow denies coercing anyone to fight in Ukraine.
They indicate that Russia is struggling for manpower.
The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, posted an analysis of the leaked data, saying the figures likely understate Russia’s true losses because of reporting limitations.
It added that, as of July, Russia’s casualties are now outpacing its recruitment.
Kluge told The Moscow Times that the deaths also represent about half a per cent of Russia’s working-age population, which may have little economic impact, so the main significance is political.
He added, “You cannot say Russia is winning this war if it is losing population at this rate.”

articles.title_orig: ISRAEL/PALESTINE: Statement by the High Representative on behalf of the European Union on the humanitarian developments in Gaza
articles.title_zh: ISRAEL/PALESTINE: Statement by the High Representative on behalf of the European Union on the humanitarian developments in Gaza
articles.content_orig:
The European Union has urged Israel to reopen all Gaza border crossings and grant “immediate, unimpeded access” for aid groups to provide humanitarian relief in the territory following devastating flooding in Gaza this week.
Civilian infrastructure and medical facilities in Gaza “must be protected,” said an EU statement released on Saturday by the office of Kaja Kallas, the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and the Vice-President of the European Commission.
The EU call came as an Israeli drone attack killed two more Palestinians in Gaza on Saturday.
The drone struck them as they walked down a street in Jabaliya on the northern edge of Gaza City, according to Mohamed Abu Selmiya, director of Shifa Hospital in Gaza City, where the casualties were taken. The American field hospital said several other people were wounded but did not provide a number.
The Israeli military said it struck two Hamas “militants” in the area.
An Israeli air attack on Thursday at the Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza killed at least six Palestinians, including a surgeon, and left dozens wounded.
“The EU underlines the need to respect international law, including international humanitarian law, at all times,” the 27-nation bloc said on Saturday. “This includes the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as medical personnel and facilities. The recent airstrike on the Nasser Hospital is deeply alarming,” it added.
Damage from Israeli attacks on Gaza’s infrastructure has worsened floods caused by heavy rain, which have submerged large areas of the enclave, local officials and the UN said this week. Gaza’s media office reported that more than 700km of Gaza’s sewage network has been destroyed.
Heavy rain has directly affected at least 106,000 people in Gaza in recent days, according to the UN children’s agency, UNICEF, with thousands of tents for displaced Palestinians submerged and latrines overflowing into camps.
In response, the EU said that “Israel must enable the work of the UN and its agencies, and humanitarian organisations including NGOs, and comply with all its obligations under international law, including international humanitarian law and international human rights law.”
The EU reaffirmed “its commitment to the two-state solution” and called for “the full withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza” as it called for “sustained distribution of humanitarian assistance and early recovery support at scale” to ease the worsening humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
